x: The rules changed. Here's what nobody told you. Most students who struggle in their first year of college are smart enough. What trips them up is that the rules changed, and nobody told them how, or how much. High school and college are both called "school," and they look similar from the outside. But how they work, what they expect from you, and what happens when you fall short are very different. This lesson makes those differences visible so you can navigate them instead of running into them the hard way. No matter where you're coming from (straight out of high school, a dual enrollment program, years in the workforce, or somewhere in between), this is worth your full attention.

Who's in this room OCTC classrooms, online and in person, bring together students from very different places. Two of the most common are students coming from high school and students returning to education after time in the workforce. The expectations in this lesson apply to everyone, but they land differently depending on where you're starting. If you're coming from high school You may have been an excellent student. You may have earned high grades, taken advanced courses, and had teachers who knew your name and followed up when you were struggling. In college, the support is still here, but you have to go looking for it. Nobody will chase you down for a missing assignment, because you're expected to manage your own academic life as an adult, even if you're 16 or 17. The adjustment has less to do with ability than with habits: following through, following directions, and taking ownership. If you're returning after time away You may have been out of school for years, maybe decades. You've been managing real responsibilities: jobs, families, finances, communities. That experience works in your favor. The professional habits you've built (showing up, communicating clearly, following through on commitments) are exactly what college expects. You already know more about accountability than you might think. The adjustment is often the systems: Blackboard, academic language, citation formats, the pace of a semester. All of that can be learned, and you're bringing a solid foundation to build on.

s: The big shift: responsibility moves to you
x: The big shift: responsibility moves to you In high school, the system was designed to catch you. In college, the system is designed to support you, but only if you engage with it. This is the most important difference, and it shows up everywhere. In high school, teachers often remind you about deadlines, follow up when you're absent, and give you chances to redo work. In college, those things still exist, but they're your job to start, not your instructor's job to offer. Before Your teacher reminded you about the assignment due Friday. If you missed it, they asked you what happened. Now The due date is in the syllabus. If you're going to miss it, you reach out first, before the deadline, not after. Before If you didn't understand something, your teacher noticed and checked in with you. Now If you don't understand something, you go to office hours, email your instructor, or visit the Teaching & Learning Center. You start the conversation. Before You could skim the directions and still do well because you had a sense of what was expected. Now Directions are specific and intentional. Not following them can cost you points, even on a strong piece of work, so read everything. Before Your relationship with your teacher was ongoing. They knew you over time and gave you the benefit of the doubt. Now Your instructor may have 30, 60, or 150 students. They'll learn who you are through how you show up: your work, your communication, your follow-through.

s: The syllabus is a contract. Read it that way.
x: The syllabus is a contract. Read it that way. Every course you take has a syllabus . Most students skim it once and never look at it again, which is one of the most common first-year mistakes. Your syllabus tells you exactly what's expected, how you'll be graded, what happens if you miss a deadline, how to contact your instructor, and what the academic integrity policy is for that course. If something goes wrong and you say you didn't know, the first question will be whether it was in the syllabus. For FYE 100, the Syllabus Acknowledgement you completed before Module 1 checked the parts students most often miss. Use the same habits in every course you take. Read it before the first week is over. Read the policies section too, not only the assignment schedule. Note every deadline. Put them in your phone, your planner, or your weekly map instead of trusting yourself to remember. Find the late work policy. Some instructors accept late work with a penalty and some don't. Know which one you're dealing with before it matters. Find the communication policy. How does your instructor want to be contacted? How quickly do they respond? Do they hold office hours? Find the AI policy. It varies from course to course. Key term Syllabus: the document that lays out a course's expectations, grading, deadlines, and policies. Each course has its own. Pathfinder Tip When something in the syllabus is unclear, ask before you act on your assumption. "I read the syllabus and wasn't sure how X works. Can you help me understand?" is a professional way to ask, and it shows you actually read it. See also Lesson 1.4: Navigating AI Policies covers how AI rules differ between courses.

s: What instructors expect (that they don't always say out loud)
x: What instructors expect (that they don't always say out loud) Four expectations come up in almost every college course. None of them is complicated, but all of them are easy to miss if nobody points them out. Follow the directions, all of them Assignment directions exist for a reason. Word counts, formatting requirements, citation styles, and submission formats aren't arbitrary. They reflect what the instructor is actually assessing. Submitting excellent content without following the directions tells your instructor you either didn't read them or decided they didn't apply to you. This is one of the most common places strong students trip up in their first semester. The work is good, but points are lost for something entirely preventable. Pathfinder Tip Before you submit anything, reread the directions one more time and check your work against each stated requirement. Ask "does this meet every requirement?" rather than "does this seem right?" Communicate like a professional Email to your instructor is professional communication, not a text message. That means a subject line, a greeting, complete sentences, and a signature. It also means being specific about what you need instead of saying something is confusing. Instead of this "hey i was confused about the assignment" Try this "Professor [Name], I'm working on this week's reflection assignment and want to make sure I understand Question 3. I read it as asking for [your interpretation]. Is that right, or am I missing something? Thank you for your time." The second version tells your instructor exactly what you need, shows you've already tried to figure it out, and treats them as a professional. Aim for that every time. See also Module 2 goes deeper on professional email. Manage your own deadlines Deadlines in college are real. Life happens, and most instructors are human about genuine emergencies. But "I forgot" or "I didn't realize it was due" is a planning problem, not an emergency, and it's yours to own. If something comes up that affects your ability to meet a deadline, reach out to your instructor before the deadline, not after. Most instructors are far more willing to work with a student who communicated early than one who disappeared and came back with an explanation after the fact. Pathfinder Tip An email the day before a deadline explaining a problem shows ownership. An email the day after asking for an exception asks your instructor to absorb the cost of your planning. Academic integrity is non-negotiable Academic integrity means your work represents your own thinking, effort, and understanding. It means citing sources when you use someone else's ideas. It means not submitting work that someone else, or an AI, produced as if it were your own. It means being honest about what you did and didn't do. The consequences for academic integrity violations in college are serious, and they can follow you. Think it through before you make a decision you can't undo. Every course has an academic integrity policy, and many also have a specific AI policy. Read both. When you're unsure whether something crosses a line, ask your instructor before you do it, not after. Key term Academic integrity: doing your own work, giving credit to others' ideas, and being honest about how your work was produced.

Owning your own learning Everything in this lesson comes back to one idea: in college, you are the person most responsible for your academic success. More than your instructor, your advisor, or your family, it's you. That can feel like a lot. It also means you have more say over your college experience than you've ever had over your education. You choose how much effort you put in, how much support you seek, and what you take away from each course. The students who do well in college often weren't the best prepared coming in. They figured out how college works, and then they used what they learned. Reflect Look back at the four "Before / Now" shifts. Which one will take the most adjustment for you, and what's one thing you could do this week to get ahead of it? You don't have to have all of this figured out on day one, and nobody does. Start paying attention now, though, because the habits you build in your first few weeks tend to stick.

What Kentucky says every college graduate should be able to do, and where you're headed. Every college in Kentucky's public system, including OCTC, uses the same framework to describe what a college education should develop in you. It's called the Kentucky Graduate Profile, and at its center are 10 Essential Skills. These are the skills that show up in every job posting, every performance review, and every meaningful challenge you'll face after college. FYE 100 is built around them. Use this page as a reference. Skim it now, before your Skills Snapshot. You'll come back to it all semester, because each module spotlights one or more of these skills, and your STAR(T) Stories capstone is built on them. Go to the source Read the full Kentucky Graduate Profile from the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education.

The 10 Essential Skills You'll use every one of these well beyond the classroom. 1 Communication Listening carefully, responding clearly, and expressing your ideas in writing, conversation, and presentations in ways that land. 2 Critical & Creative Thinking Questioning assumptions, evaluating information, and coming up with new ideas or better solutions instead of accepting the first answer. 3 Quantitative Reasoning Using numbers and data to make sense of problems and reach informed conclusions, whether that's a budget, a chart, or a statistic in the news. 4 Interpersonal Relations Understanding yourself and others, and working respectfully with people who think, live, and communicate differently than you do. 5 Adaptability & Leadership Adjusting when things change, staying effective under pressure, and helping others move toward a goal, even when you're not in charge. 6 Professionalism Acting with integrity, managing your time, taking initiative, and being accountable for your work: the habits that define a reliable person in any field. 7 Civic Engagement Participating in your community and the broader world as someone who contributes to making things better, rather than watching from the sidelines. 8 Collaboration & Teamwork Showing up reliably for a group, managing disagreement constructively, and making the team stronger. 9 Knowledge Application Taking what you've learned and actually using it: connecting academic content to real situations in your career and your life. 10 Information Literacy Finding, evaluating, and responsibly using information to make good decisions, especially in a world full of sources that aren't all trustworthy.

s: Where you're starting, and where you're headed
x: Where you're starting, and where you're headed Kentucky describes these skills at three levels. Most students start college around Benchmark and work toward Milestone over two years of college. Key term Milestone: the level Kentucky expects after two years of college, when you can use a skill on your own in real situations. Benchmark Where students typically are when they start college. You're beginning to develop these skills, often with some guidance or support still needed. Roughly equivalent to high school completion. Milestone Your target Where you should be after two years of college. You can demonstrate each skill independently, in real situations, without being told exactly how. Expected at associate degree completion or halfway through a bachelor's program. Capstone Where bachelor's degree graduates should be: applying each skill with expertise and precision in professional and civic settings. Expected at bachelor's degree completion.

Tracking your own growth You don't need to master all 10 skills in one semester. FYE 100 is the starting point: a chance to name the skills, see what they look like in practice, and start building the habits that carry you toward Milestone. In Blackboard, you'll rate yourself on these skills, and on how you use AI, with the My Skills Snapshot near the start of the course. You'll take it again at the end, then compare the two. The goal is an honest starting point you can measure your growth against later, not a high score now. At the end of the course, you'll write or record three short STAR(T) Stories: one for each of two assigned skills (Professionalism and Knowledge Application) and one for a skill you choose. STAR(T) is a structured way to tell a story that shows a skill in action, using real experiences from your own life, and the groundwork starts here. You can write your stories or record them, and recording is worth a try. Telling a story out loud, in your own voice, is the closest practice you'll get for how you'll actually use it: in a job interview, a scholarship conversation, or any time someone asks, "Tell me about a time when…" Pathfinder Tip When you rate yourself, be honest rather than generous. A realistic starting point makes your growth easier to see.

AI is already part of your daily life. This lesson is about using it thoughtfully. You already use AI. You may not call it that, but you do. Every time you ask a voice assistant something, get a "you might also like" recommendation, or see a summary at the top of a search page, something behind the scenes is deciding what you see. That something is artificial intelligence. AI isn't a robot, and it isn't magic. The chat tools most people mean when they say "AI" are systems trained on enormous amounts of human-written text. They've gotten very good at producing responses that sound confident, authoritative, and complete. Key term Artificial intelligence (AI): computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human thinking, like answering questions, writing, or recognizing patterns. Sounding confident isn't the same as being right. AI doesn't know you. It doesn't know your situation, your goals, or whether the answer it just gave you actually applies to your life. It produces what's statistically likely to be useful, which is often helpful and occasionally very, very wrong.

s: The part that trips people up
x: The part that trips people up AI doesn't get things wrong the way a broken calculator does. Here's a better way to picture it. Try it Hum this bassline: bum, bum, bum, buttabum, bum… (Bear with me.) Now ask a few different people what song it is. Some will say Queen and David Bowie's "Under Pressure." Others, depending on their age and what they grew up with, will say Vanilla Ice's "Ice Ice Baby." Neither person is wrong. They both recognized a real pattern and completed it in the direction that was most familiar to them. That's surprisingly close to what an AI chat tool does. Instead of looking up a fact and checking whether it's true, it recognizes patterns in language and produces the most likely next words, based on everything it was trained on. Most of the time, that's accurate and useful. But sometimes the answer that sounds most likely isn't the correct one; it's just the one that fits the pattern best. When AI produces something that sounds completely believable but isn't true, it's called a hallucination . Hallucinations aren't a glitch that will eventually go away. They happen when a pattern-completing system runs into a gap and fills it with whatever fits. So when something an AI tells you seems off, "did it make a mistake?" is the wrong question. A better one is: that sounded right, but is sounding right the same as being right? That's why how you use AI matters more than whether you use it. Key term Hallucination: when AI produces information that sounds believable but is false, such as a fact, quote, or source that doesn't exist.

s: Five ways to show up thoughtfully
x: Five ways to show up thoughtfully This course uses five behaviors to describe what thoughtful AI use looks like. You'll see them throughout the book. Two of them, BE Critical and BE Reflective, come up again and again, because they're the habits that travel with you into every course, every job, and every situation where someone is trying to tell you something. BE Safe Know what you're sharing and with whom. Your personal information, financial details, and private circumstances stay private. BE Honest There's a real difference between getting help from a tool and letting a tool do your thinking for you. Be clear about which one you're doing. BE Critical Don't take AI output at face value. Check it. Ask where it came from. Notice when something seems off. This is the most transferable habit you'll build. BE Responsible Make intentional choices about when AI supports your learning and when it gets in the way. Telling the two apart takes practice. BE Reflective Notice what happens to your thinking when you use AI. Are you learning more, or less? Are you more confident in your own ideas, or less? These five behaviors describe who you want to be as an AI user. The next lesson turns them into something you can do, every time you use AI for coursework. In Blackboard, the BE Check asks you to match each behavior to a real situation. See also Lesson 1.4: Navigating AI Policies puts these behaviors into practice.

Your choice to make You don't have to love AI, and you don't have to use it. What this course asks is simpler: think before you act, and pay attention to what you're learning and how. That goes for AI, and for everything else in this book, too. Pathfinder Tip If you want to explore, start with Microsoft Copilot. It comes with your KCTCS Microsoft Office 365 account, so you sign in with your student login.

Every course sets its own AI rules. Here's how to find them, and a routine for using AI well. There's no single AI rule for college. Each course, and sometimes each assignment, sets its own. In one course, you might be encouraged to brainstorm with AI. In another, using AI at all could count as an academic integrity violation. Both can be true in the same week. This lesson shows you where to find the rules, what to do when they aren't clear, and a simple routine to use any time you work with AI.

Where to find the rules Look in two places, in this order. The AI Course Policy Look for the AI Course Policy section of your syllabus. It explains your instructor's overall approach to AI for that course. The assignment instructions Each assignment has an AI use label. The label tells you how AI can be used on that specific piece of work. See also Lesson 1.1 on reading your syllabus like a contract. Three AI use labels Assignments use one of three labels. Think of them as points on one scale, from no AI at all to AI as part of the assignment itself. No AI You do this work on your own. Your instructor chose this because the skill itself is what you're practicing. Example: a short quiz that checks what you know on your own. AI-supported You can use AI for the parts your instructor names, like brainstorming or checking grammar. The thinking and the final work are yours. Example: using Copilot to brainstorm topic ideas, then choosing one and writing the paper yourself. AI-integrated Using AI well is part of the assignment. You might check what AI gives you against a standard, or explain how you used it. Example: asking AI a question, checking its answer against your textbook, and explaining what it got right and wrong. Labels are chosen assignment by assignment , not for a whole course. The same course can have one assignment at No AI and the next at AI-integrated. Check the assignment instructions every time. What an AI use label looks like at the top of an assignment ● ○ AI use: AI-supported You may use AI to brainstorm ideas. Your response must be written in your own words. See the AI Course Policy in the syllabus. If an assignment doesn't have an AI use label, or you aren't sure what it means, ask your instructor instead of guessing. A Note from a Pathfinder How other Pathfinders used AI Walk me through it One student got stuck on a problem and asked AI to walk them through it. They said it helped them understand more, and they noticed they were taking more notes than they had at the start of the semester. I changed my mind about what kind of help is okay Another student started the semester thinking AI had no place in schoolwork. By the end, they could see a role for it in brainstorming and organizing ideas, when the assignment allows that kind of help. Adapted from two previous FYE students' reflections Before you use AI, ask: What kind of help am I allowed to use on this assignment? Check the label: No AI, AI-supported, or AI-integrated. If AI is allowed, try this prompt: I'm stuck on this step. Help me figure out what I'm missing, then let me try the next step myself.

When the rules aren't clear Ask before you use AI, not after. An instructor can easily answer a question before you start. It's much harder to sort things out once work has been turned in. Try asking like this "Professor [Name], the directions for [assignment] don't mention AI. Would it be okay to use Copilot to brainstorm topic ideas if I write the paper myself?" A specific question gets a specific answer. It also shows your instructor that you take the rules seriously.

The 3 Qs Once you know the rules, three questions keep you on track. Each one belongs to a moment in your work. Before you ask AI Should I use AI for this part of my assignment? BE Responsible · BE Honest Before you use AI's answer How would I know if AI's answer is wrong? BE Critical Before you turn in your work Can I explain my work and how AI helped me? BE Honest · BE Reflective Notice the behaviors under each question. The 3 Qs are the five behaviors from Lesson 1.3 turned into a routine. The fifth, BE Safe, applies every time: never paste other people's personal information, passwords, or anything private into an AI tool. Pathfinder Tip When AI is optional, choosing not to use it is a good choice too.

Keep a trail A trail is a record of how your work grew over time. If your instructor asks how you did an assignment, you can show them. Tools that try to spot AI writing are sometimes wrong, and your trail is real evidence of your own work. It also lets you say exactly how AI helped you. Write in Word, saved to OneDrive. Word keeps a dated history of your draft as you write. Type your work in the document instead of pasting it in at the end. Keep a OneNote notebook for each course. Save your notes, sources, and ideas there while you work. Write down how you use AI. Copy your question into OneNote and note what you kept, changed, or left out. See also Trail Tip: Your Free Microsoft Office 365 Access shows how to get Word, OneDrive, and OneNote. Keep a Trail in OCTC Student Resources walks through setup and shows a sample notebook page.

Take it with you OCTC Student Resources has an AI Literacy page with the same labels, the same 3 Qs, and a page for each question with checks and examples. It works for every course you take here, so bookmark it. Open AI Literacy in Student Resources Try it Open the syllabus for one of your other courses this semester. Find its AI Course Policy, then look at one assignment's AI use label. What does it allow, and is anything unclear enough that you'd want to ask your instructor?

The basics you need to navigate your courses with confidence. Blackboard Ultra is where your courses live: your assignments, your grades, your instructor's feedback, and your connection to your classmates. Use this page as a reference. Skim it now, and come back whenever you can't find something in Blackboard. It doesn't take long to learn, and knowing where things are from the start makes a real difference. This lesson covers the handful of things you need in your first week. For everything else, you'll find two help resources at the end.

1 Set up your profile Before you do anything else, add a profile photo. Online courses can feel anonymous, and a photo changes that. It tells your instructor and classmates that there's a real person on the other end of the screen, and it makes discussions feel more like actual conversations. You don't need a professional headshot. A clear, recent photo where people can see your face is all it takes. Select your avatar or initials in the top-right corner of any Blackboard page. Select Profile from the menu. Select the profile image area and upload a photo from your device. Save your changes. Pathfinder Tip While you're in your profile, make sure your name appears the way you want your instructors and classmates to see it.

2 Find your way around Inside each course, a menu takes you to the main areas you'll use every week: Course Content Home base. Your modules, lessons, and assignments are listed here in order, top to bottom. Open a module to see everything inside it. Most weeks, this is where you'll start. Calendar What's coming up in this course: assignment due dates, plus class meetings if your instructor has added them. Switch to the Due Dates view to see your assignments listed in order, soonest first. Gradebook Your grades for everything you've submitted, plus what's still ahead. Select any item to see your score and the feedback your instructor left. (More on feedback in step 5.) Messages Private messages between you and your instructor or classmates, sent inside the course. It's a quick way to ask your instructor a question about this class. Some instructors prefer email, so check your syllabus. Announcements Updates from your instructor: reminders, changes, and heads-ups. New announcements often appear when you open the course, and they're also sent to your KCTCS email. Check these regularly. One calendar for all your courses The Calendar inside a course shows only that course. For the big picture, go to the main Blackboard page you see right after you log in, before you open any course, and select Calendar from the menu there. That calendar pulls in due dates from all of your courses at once, color-coded by course, so you can see a busy week coming before you're in the middle of it. Pathfinder Tip Every instructor organizes modules a little differently. Spend a few minutes clicking through the first module of each course to learn its pattern.

3 Submit your work Assignments in Blackboard Ultra are submitted through the course, not by email. Most follow the same steps: Open the assignment from its module. Read the instructions carefully before you start. Type your response in the text box, or attach a file if the assignment calls for one. Select Submit when you're done. You'll see a confirmation that your work was received. Pathfinder Tip Don't wait until the last minute to submit. Technical issues happen, and submitting early gives you time to fix them.

4 Take part in discussions Discussions usually work in two parts: your first post, and your replies to classmates. Many discussions have two separate deadlines , one for each part. Check the discussion in Blackboard for the exact dates. Open the discussion from its module. Select Add a Response to write your first post. After posting, read what your classmates have written. Reply to classmates by the reply deadline. Pathfinder Tip Replies are usually graded too. A reply that responds to something specific your classmate said is worth far more than "great point, I agree."

5 Read your instructor's feedback After your instructor grades your work, they often leave written feedback along with your score. It's one of the most valuable parts of a course and one of the most commonly ignored. Your instructor took time to write it. In an online class, it's the closest thing you get to a one-on-one conversation, so read it. Go to the Gradebook . Select the assignment you want to review. Look for written comments alongside your score. If something is unclear, use Messages to follow up with your instructor. Pathfinder Tip Feedback on early assignments tells you exactly what your instructor values. Reading it closely can change how you approach everything that comes after.

6 Stay in the loop Instructors post announcements throughout the semester: reminders, clarifications, encouragement, and updates. Announcements appear in your course and are also sent to your KCTCS email. Make a habit of checking both. Missing an announcement is one of the most common reasons students are caught off guard by a change. Pathfinder Tip Set up your KCTCS email on your phone. It's the official channel for everything at OCTC: announcements, financial aid, registration, all of it. Go deeper: Blackboard Ultra video tutorials Short how-to videos on navigation, assignments, discussions, grades, and more. Bookmark it; you'll use it more than once. Open the playlist on YouTube Look it up: Blackboard Help for Students Blackboard's official help pages for students, with step-by-step instructions for getting started, course content, assignments and tests, grades, and the Blackboard app. When you're stuck on how to do something, search here. Interacting effectively with people, and understanding what you bring to every relationship. 4 10 Essential Skills · #4 Interpersonal Relations

What this skill is Interpersonal Relations is about more than being friendly. It's the ability to understand yourself well enough to interact effectively with others. Your background, experiences, and perspective shape every conversation you have. This skill means seeing that, and respecting people who see things differently than you do. In college, at work, and in life, the people around you will be different from you in ways that matter. This skill is what lets you work alongside them, and learn from them.

Where you're headed Kentucky describes this skill at different levels. Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You can describe your own perspective and experiences. You recognize that other people have different perspectives than yours. You understand that those differences affect how people interact. Milestone Your target You can explain how your own background and experiences shape your relationships, not just that they do. You actively look for positive ways to connect and work with others. You engage with multiple perspectives, ideas, and beliefs instead of noticing them from a distance. You don't have to become a different person to move from Benchmark to Milestone. What grows is your awareness of how you show up, and your intention to show up well.

Mapping your support team means looking honestly at your relationships: who's in your corner, how they help, and what makes it hard to lean on them. Asking for help means getting past what usually gets in the way, which is almost always interpersonal: pride, fear of judgment, or not knowing how to ask. Talking with classmates whose situations are different from yours, and engaging with what they actually said, is how this skill grows.

In your own life You don't have to write anything down. Just sit with these questions for a moment. Reflect Think about a relationship that matters to you: a friend, a family member, a coworker. How has your background or experience shaped how you show up in that relationship? Is there someone in your life whose perspective is very different from yours? What have you learned from that difference, or what has made it hard? When you think about asking for help, what gets in the way? Is any of that connected to how you see yourself in relation to other people?

Asking for help is a skill successful students use every day. College can feel like a long trail with steep climbs and unexpected turns, but no one reaches the summit alone. Successful students know when and how to ask for help, and that's a sign of confidence and self-awareness, not weakness. Reaching out early keeps small challenges from becoming big obstacles. The students who struggle most usually aren't the ones who know the least; they're the ones who wait too long to ask.

What help-seeking really means It's more than raising your hand in class. Help-seeking means using your resources, relationships, and communication skills to stay on track before things go sideways. It can look like: Asking a classmate to study together. Emailing your instructor when you're confused about an assignment. Meeting with your Success Coach to talk about goals or time management. Visiting tutoring or the library for extra support on a specific skill. Reaching out to financial aid or counseling when life gets complicated. Each of these takes initiative, which is the opposite of giving up. Key term Help-seeking: reaching out to people and resources on purpose, before a small problem becomes a big one.

Four tips for confident help-seeking You already know how to do this. When your car makes a noise you don't recognize, you ask someone. When a shift gets switched on you, you text the person who can fix it. You already have this skill. College just gives you new places to use it. With people you trust, you probably already ask early, get specific, and follow through. The tip that's new is communicating professionally, because the relationship is different. Ask early Don't wait until you're overwhelmed. A question early in the semester is easier to answer than a crisis near the end. Be specific Instead of "I don't get this," try "I'm confused about this part. Could you walk me through another example?" Specific questions get specific help. Communicate professionally Be polite, be clear, and sign your name. Your instructors and advisors are colleagues, not customer service. You wouldn't text your instructor the way you text your cousin. It's the same skill in a different setting. Follow through Use the advice you get. If someone helps you, let them know how it went. That's how professional relationships are built. See also Lesson 2.4 shows what a clear, specific request looks like in an email.

Communicate professionally College email isn't like texting. It reflects your professional self, and instructors notice the difference. The same goes for everything you write in a course: discussion posts, journals, and the AI Chats with Coach Pathfinder. It's all course communication, and your instructor reads it. 1 Address people correctly Use a respectful title and last name: Professor, Dr., Mr., or Ms. Don't use first names unless your instructor has said it's okay. When in doubt, "Professor" works for any college instructor. 2 Write a subject line The subject line is the short title you type in the Subject box, above your message. It's the first thing your instructor sees in their inbox, before they open your email. Not this Subject: hi can u tell me if the reflection is due friday or monday because i work friday Not this either Subject: (blank) or Subject: Question This Subject: FYE 100 Section 201: Question About Reflection Due Date A good subject line is short, specific, and includes your course. Your instructor can tell what you need before opening the email, and can find it again later. Key term Subject line: the short title of an email. It tells the reader what the email is about. The message itself goes in the body below. 3 Write a clear, complete message Every professional email has the same basic parts. Skip text shortcuts, emojis, and slang, even if your instructor seems casual in class. Greeting "Hello Dr. Smith," Introduction "My name is Jordan Lee, and I'm in your online FYE 100, Section 201." Purpose "I wanted to ask whether the reflection assignment has a rubric." Closing "Thank you," followed by your full name 4 Stay respectful and calm If you're upset about a grade, a deadline, or a situation, step away before you reply. Reread your email out loud and ask yourself: would I say this in person? Once you hit Send, you can't take the words back. Your instructor is a real person who wants to help you succeed. 5 Be specific and prepared Your instructor may be working with more than 100 students this semester. The more your email tells them up front, the faster they can help. Include the course name and section number in every email. Instructors often teach several sections. Check the syllabus and announcements first . Your question may already be answered there, and showing that you looked goes a long way.

See the difference Not this Subject: Hey can u tell me how to do number 4 on the problem set. i no u went over it in class but i have had a VERY LONG week lol tests ha ha ha and i lost my notes. pleeease help Stu This Subject: Question About Reflection Assignment Instructions Dear Professor Brown, I hope you're having a good start to the week! I'm in your FYE 100, Section 203, that meets on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I wanted to ask for clarification about the reflection assignment. I've reviewed the syllabus, my notes, and the course announcements, and I also checked with a classmate. I think the reflection is supposed to be posted to a separate portal, but I want to make sure before I submit. Could you please confirm where we should post it? Thank you for your time and help! Sincerely, Jordan Lee

Tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, and the AI Chats in this course are all powered by a large language model : an AI system trained on enormous amounts of text, so it can predict and generate language that sounds clear and relevant. On its own, it's a very capable generalist. It has read more text than any person ever could, and it can discuss almost any topic. But it doesn't know who you are, what class you're in, or what you're supposed to be thinking about today. Until someone gives it direction, it's just potential. An AI is only as useful as the directions it's been given. Look back at Lesson 1.3: What's AI, Really?

Those instructions tell it how to behave in this specific chat. For the AI Chats in this course, the instructions come from the setup in Blackboard: the type of chat, the topic, the coach's name and personality, how it should respond, and how complex its answers should be. Blackboard turns those choices into instructions the AI reads first, and they shape everything that happens next. Key term System prompt : the hidden instructions an AI reads before a conversation starts. Almost every AI tool has one. Below is a simplified example of what those instructions might say for one of the chats in this course. It isn't the exact setup, but it's close. Simplified example: how Coach Pathfinder gets set up Role: You are Coach Pathfinder, a warm, direct coach for first-year college students at OCTC. Purpose: Help this student think through their support network and what it means to ask for help. Ask questions that help them find their own answers. Tone: Encouraging but honest. Treat the student as capable. Don't be generic or vague. Opening: Welcome the student and ask: "When things get hard in college, what's your instinct: push through alone, or reach out? Tell me about that." Rule: "Do not write the student's answers for them. Your job is to help them find what they already know." Guardrails: Stay on the topic. If the student asks you to do their homework, guide them back to reflecting. The same AI that could draft a legal brief or explain quantum physics has been given one specific job, and it does that job every time a student opens that chat.

Being reliable, accountable, and intentional, not perfect. 6 10 Essential Skills · #6 Professionalism

What this skill is Professionalism can sound vague, like something that happens in an office somewhere, after college, when you're wearing different clothes. Kentucky's definition is more specific and more immediate than that. Professionalism means acting with honesty and fairness, managing your time and tasks, taking initiative, and being accountable for your own actions, including your mistakes. Professionalism is a pattern of behavior, not a performance, and that pattern either builds or erodes trust over time. It starts right now, in how you show up for this course. Professionalism means being someone people can count on, not being perfect.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You treat people honestly and fairly in your interactions. You know that deadlines and punctuality matter for success. You follow through on obligations and commitments. You're curious about professional fields and what they require. Milestone Your target You can describe what ethical behavior looks like, and you make choices that reflect it. You use organization and time management skills to prioritize and complete tasks, not just intend to. You take personal accountability for your actions, including when things go wrong. You communicate using the language and tools of your field. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from knowing what professionalism looks like to doing it consistently, including when it isn't easy.

Professionalism means working with how you actually function, not grinding through exhaustion.

Before the week runs you, run the week. Students who fall behind usually care. What happened is that Monday arrived before they knew what it was going to ask of them. A weekly map doesn't solve everything, but it means you're never caught completely off guard. You don't need a perfect schedule. You need five minutes at the start of the week to see what you're actually dealing with, so you can make better decisions when the week gets complicated. The goal is a plan that helps you recover faster when things go sideways, not one you follow perfectly.

Look back, then look ahead This module gives you two tools, and they do different jobs. Tracking is looking back: an honest record of where your time and energy actually went. Planning is looking ahead: deciding where your time should go next week. You need the first to do the second well. A plan built on the week you wish you had won't survive the week you actually have. Look back: Where My Time Goes A reality check . Log what actually happened with your time and energy, day by day. No judging, no fixing yet. Just notice. Use it for: Mile Marker #3, Question 1 Open Where My Time Goes Look ahead: My Week at a Glance A plan . Use what you learned from looking back to map your priorities into the week ahead. Use it for: Mile Marker #3, Question 3 Open My Week at a Glance

s: Map your week in three steps
x: Map your week in three steps 1 Name your priorities before you touch the calendar Before you look at a single time slot, answer one question: What absolutely has to happen this week? Then sort your priorities into three buckets. Must Non-negotiable. Missing this has real consequences. Should Important, but could flex if something urgent comes up. Could Nice to do, but it won't derail your week if it waits. Most students have two or three Musts, a handful of Shoulds, and a long list of Coulds they'll never get to, and that's normal. The point is knowing which is which before the week decides for you. Pathfinder Tip If everything feels like a Must, it isn't. Push back on yourself. What actually has a deadline? What actually has consequences? Start there. 2 Know your energy before you block your time Before you drop anything into a time block, ask yourself: When am I actually sharp this week? Not when you think you should be productive, but when you actually are. Are you a morning person or a night owl? Does your energy crash after lunch? Do you need a slow start before you hit your stride? Put your most important work in your best hours. Don't schedule a hard assignment for the time of day when you're running on empty. Pathfinder Tip Your best hours are your most valuable resource. Protect them the way you'd protect a meeting with someone important, because you are someone important. 3 Block broadly, and leave white space Place your Musts and Shoulds into a morning, afternoon, and evening grid. You don't need to schedule every hour. Anchor your priorities to the times you're most likely to do them. Then leave gaps. White space is where you handle the unexpected, move between tasks, eat lunch without rushing, and remember that you're a person, not a productivity machine. Weekends are for rest as well as catching up. Plan them that way on purpose. Buffer time between commitments is part of the plan, not a failure of the plan. If every block is full, something won't happen. Decide in advance what flexes. Pathfinder Tip A plan with white space is more realistic than a packed plan, and a realistic plan is the only kind that works.

What gets in the way These are the most common planning mistakes, and what to do instead. Mistake Planning from empty boxes. Filling in a schedule without knowing your priorities first. The schedule looks full, but nothing important is protected. Instead Priorities first, schedule second. Name your Musts before you touch the calendar. Then place them in your best hours. Mistake Planning for your best self. Scheduling six hours of focused study on a day you work a full shift and have a family commitment. It won't happen. Instead Planning for your real self. Be honest about what's actually possible each day. A small, realistic plan beats a big, aspirational one every time. Mistake Treating the plan like a contract. When something disrupts the plan, giving up entirely because "the week is ruined." One missed block isn't a failed week. Instead Using the plan to recover. When something shifts, look at the plan and ask: what's the next best move? The plan helps you recover. It doesn't have to be followed perfectly. Lookout: Ask Your Success Coach If you've mapped your week honestly and the hours still don't fit, talk with your Success Coach. Your coach can help you decide whether to adjust your plan or change your schedule. After the add period ends, you can't swap one course for another. Your options are usually to withdraw from a course, and possibly to add a shorter bi-term course. Either one can affect your financial aid, so talk with your coach before you make a change. Your coach can also help you choose a course load for next semester that fits your schedule. Not sure who your coach is? Lesson 2.2 shows you how to find them.

Five minutes to start Students who manage their time well still get overwhelmed. The difference is that they know what they're dealing with before it overwhelms them, and they have a map to find their way back when it does. Getting started takes five minutes on Sunday evening or Monday morning. t: Run the Day (Don't Let It Run You)
x: Small, intentional decisions, made consistently, are how the day becomes yours. "The bad news is time flies. The good news is you're the pilot." Michael Altshuler You've heard "time flies" your whole life, usually as the reason something didn't happen: the assignment that didn't get done, the week that got away, the semester that's almost over before you noticed it going. Time doesn't fly on its own, though. Days fill up because we let them, with the urgent instead of the important, the easy instead of the necessary, and the scroll instead of the start. You're already in the cockpit, and the question is whether you're flying the plane or along for the ride. This lesson covers four small moves that help you run the day instead of letting the day run you.

t: Run the Day (Don't Let It Run You)
s: Four moves that keep you in the cockpit
x: Four moves that keep you in the cockpit 1 Find your best hour, and protect it Every day you have at least one window when your brain is working well. Maybe it's first thing in the morning, before everything else starts pulling at you. Maybe it's late evening, when the house is finally quiet. Maybe it's the 45 minutes between classes when you're already in the zone. That window is the most valuable part of your day, so learn when it is and save it for your most important work. Watch for the time-wasters that feel like breaks but quietly drain the hour before you notice it's gone: Phone scrolling. Social media, videos, anything that pulls you in. You pick it up for two minutes and look up 40 minutes later. Notification interruptions. Every buzz pulls you out of focus, and it takes longer than you think to get back in. Fake productivity. Reorganizing notes, color-coding your planner, making a to-do list instead of doing it. It feels like work, but nothing on the list gets done. Easy stuff in your best hours. Handling low-effort tasks during your peak window because they feel satisfying. Save the easy stuff for when your energy is low. Avoidance dressed up as something else. Cleaning your space, texting to stay connected, watching one more episode because the task feels too big to start. Pathfinder Tip You probably already know when your best hour is. You may even know whether you're reading this in a good window or a bad one. When your best hour arrives, put your phone face down and out of reach, even in another room if you can. 2 Start before you feel ready For almost any task, starting is harder than finishing. Your brain resists beginning something unfamiliar, uncomfortable, or uncertain, and it will find a hundred small things to do instead. That's how brains work, especially under stress, and it doesn't mean you're lazy. Avoidance often looks like something reasonable: Over-preparing. Gathering every resource and watching every tutorial before touching the actual task. Preparation becomes its own avoidance. Helping someone else first. Being genuinely useful to a friend or family member when your own work needs to happen. Doing your work first isn't selfish. The clean-space trap. The desk has to be organized, the dishes done, the room perfect before you can possibly begin. It never is. Research spirals. Looking up one thing for an assignment and ending up somewhere completely unrelated 30 minutes later. So start anyway. Open the document and write one sentence, or read the first paragraph, or do the first problem. The first two minutes are the hardest. Once you've begun, the resistance drops and the task starts to feel manageable. Pathfinder Tip If starting is hard for you most of the time, and not only once in a while, pay attention to that. It isn't a character flaw, and there are strategies that help. Look ahead Divergent Minds: Your Brain, Your Way , this module's bonus read, explains why starting is harder for some brains, and what helps. 3 Handle the small stuff when it shows up A simple rule helps here: if something takes less than two minutes, do it now. Reply to the email, submit the quick task, or send the message to your instructor. Small things that pile up are one of the most common causes of low-grade overwhelm, that feeling of always being behind without knowing why. Handle them when they show up, before they stack into a list that feels heavy before you've started. Pathfinder Tip The flip side: if something takes more than two minutes, don't start it in a two-minute window. Give it a real block in your weekly plan. Starting something you can't finish creates more mental clutter than not starting it at all. 4 Recover, don't catastrophize "Either you run the day, or the day runs you." Jim Rohn Some days go sideways. A kid gets sick, work runs long, or you sleep through your alarm, and the plan falls apart before noon. You don't have to rescue the whole day. Ask one question instead: What's the next best thing I can do right now? Not the ideal thing, and not what you would have done if the day had gone as planned, but the next good move in the situation you're actually in. A day that went sideways but ended with one task done is better than one that ended with none. Missing a block isn't failing the week. Giving up on the week after missing one block is. Recovery is a skill, and like every skill, it gets easier with practice. Pathfinder Tip Students who manage their time well still have bad days. They just recover faster. Your plan is a tool for getting back on track, not a standard you've failed to meet.

s: What running the day sounds like
x: What running the day sounds like It comes down to small decisions, made on purpose, at a few moments in the day. Morning Before I check my phone, I'm going to look at what has to happen today. Before class I have 20 minutes. I'm going to use them to start the reading, not scroll. When you're stuck I don't have to finish this. I just have to do the next small thing. When the day goes wrong What's one thing I can still do today that would make this day count? Before bed What's the one thing tomorrow needs from me? I'll put it somewhere I'll see it. End of the week What did I actually get done? What did I learn about how my week works?

t: Run the Day (Don't Let It Run You)
x: You're the pilot "Until we can manage time, we can manage nothing else." Peter Drucker Drucker saw time management as the skill underneath all the others. When your time gets away from you, everything else suffers: your grades, your relationships, your energy, and your sense of control over your own life. You don't need a perfect system. You need to decide, each day, that you're the pilot: that you're going to run the day, even imperfectly and even on the hard days, rather than let it run you. Make one good decision, and then the next one.

You're not doing two things at once. You're switching really fast, and paying for it. Most people believe they're good at multitasking. The research says that multitasking, the way we usually mean it, doesn't really exist. What we call multitasking is rapid task-switching. Your brain moves back and forth between tasks in quick succession: one thing, then another, then back to the first. It never does two at once, and every switch costs something. What feels like multitasking is task-switching, and every switch has a price.

The cost nobody talks about When you switch from one task to another, your brain doesn't just pick up where it left off. It has to reorient: figure out where it was, what it was doing, and what comes next. Researchers call this the switching cost , and it adds up faster than you'd expect. Research on interruptions has found that it can take more than 20 minutes to get back to a task after being pulled away from it. So every time you stop to check your phone, reply to a message, or flip between tabs, you may be losing far more than a few seconds. Key Term Switching cost: the time and mental effort it takes to get back up to speed after you move from one task to another.

s: Does any of this sound familiar?
x: Does any of this sound familiar? Studying "I'll just check this notification real quick…" Fifteen minutes later, you're somewhere completely different. In class You're half-listening while scrolling, then realize you missed something important and have no idea when it happened. Working on an assignment You have three tabs open, a text conversation going, and the TV on, and nothing feels like it's getting done. Getting ready to start You've been "about to start" for 45 minutes, but every time you almost begin, something pulls you away again.

s: Transition friction: why switching is harder than it looks
x: Transition friction: why switching is harder than it looks Beyond the switching cost, there's something else worth naming: transition friction . It's the resistance your brain feels when it moves from one task to another: the mental drag of leaving something unfinished, reorienting to something new, and rebuilding momentum from scratch. For most people, transition friction is a minor inconvenience. For some brains, including those with ADHD or other executive function differences, it can feel like a wall. The task itself may not be hard. Getting started on it after switching away from something else is. Key Term Transition friction: the resistance you feel when moving from one task, place, or mental state to another. If this lands harder for you If switching between tasks is noticeably more disruptive for you than it seems to be for others, that's real, and it's worth paying attention to. Some things that help: Finish a thought before you switch. Before you respond to a notification or move to a new task, write down exactly where you are and what comes next. Even one sentence makes coming back much easier. Build transitions into your plan. Don't schedule tasks back to back with no buffer. Give yourself five minutes between subjects, places, or types of work. That time is necessary, not wasted. Batch your interruptions. Instead of answering every notification as it arrives, pick specific times to check messages. Your focus stays intact in between. Pathfinder Tip Remember the phone face-down rule from Lesson 3.3 ? It's about more than willpower. Every notification that pulls you away is a task switch, and a switching cost. Face down and out of reach means fewer switches.

t: The Five Batteries: Running Low vs. Running Out
x: Understanding your energy before it's gone, and what burnout actually is. Most conversations about time management treat time like the only resource that matters. But you've probably noticed that having time isn't always enough. You can have a free afternoon and still get nothing done, not because you're lazy, but because something else is empty. That something else is energy, and energy comes in five different forms. When even one of them runs critically low, everything gets harder: focus, motivation, patience, and follow-through. Learning to recognize which battery is draining, and doing something about it before you crash, is one of the most practical self-management skills you can build. Managing your time also means managing your energy, and the two aren't the same.

t: The Five Batteries: Running Low vs. Running Out
x: The five batteries Physical Your body's fuel level: sleep, food, movement, and rest. When this battery is low, everything else suffers. You can't think clearly, manage your emotions, or stay focused on four hours of sleep and a gas station coffee. What drains it Poor or too little sleep Skipping meals or eating inconsistently Sitting for long stretches without moving Ignoring physical discomfort or illness How to recharge Protect sleep. Even 30 more minutes matters. Eat something real before a demanding task Move your body. Even a short walk changes your state. Rest without guilt when your body is asking for it Mental Your thinking capacity: focus, concentration, decision-making, and problem-solving. This battery has a daily limit. Every decision you make, every problem you think through, and every piece of information you take in draws from it. What drains it Switching between tasks constantly Information overload: too many inputs at once Making too many decisions in a short window Worry and rumination, which drain you whether the problem is real or imagined How to recharge Work in focused blocks, one thing at a time Take real breaks: actual rest, not phone breaks Cut down on small decisions by batching them or setting defaults Give your brain something easy or enjoyable to do Emotional Your capacity to handle feelings: stress, anxiety, frustration, grief, and conflict. When this battery is low, small things feel big. Patience disappears. Tasks that would normally feel manageable suddenly feel impossible. What drains it Unresolved conflict with people you care about Carrying stress without acknowledging it Pushing down emotions that need attention Financial pressure, family stress, or grief How to recharge Name what you're feeling, out loud or in writing Talk to someone you trust Do something that brings real comfort, not just distraction Reach out to counseling when what you're carrying is too heavy to carry alone Social Your capacity for connection: belonging, support, and community. This battery works differently for different people. Some people recharge through connection and need people around them to feel energized. Others recharge through solitude, and too much social time drains them, even when they enjoy it. What drains it Isolation: going too long without meaningful connection Overextension: more social obligation than fits your wiring Conflict or tension in important relationships Feeling like you don't belong somewhere you spend time How to recharge Know whether you recharge with people or alone, and plan for it Invest in one or two relationships that truly restore you Protect alone time if crowds drain you Seek connection if isolation drains you. Even a brief conversation counts. Spiritual Your sense of meaning, purpose, and alignment: the feeling that what you're doing matters, and that your values and your actions point in the same direction. This battery doesn't require religious belief. It's about the deeper question: why does any of this matter to me? When this battery is low, even tasks you're capable of feel pointless. Motivation disappears, not because you're tired, but because you've lost sight of why you're here. What drains it Doing things that feel out of line with your values Losing sight of your reasons for being in college Going through the motions without a sense of purpose Feeling like your effort doesn't lead anywhere meaningful How to recharge Reconnect with your reasons. Why did you come here? What are you working toward? Do something that fits what you value: service, creativity, faith, nature, or community Talk to someone who helps you see the bigger picture Give yourself permission to ask the big questions. They're worth asking.

t: The Five Batteries: Running Low vs. Running Out
x: What burnout actually is "Burnout" gets used loosely. "I'm so burned out" often just means tired, stressed, or overwhelmed. Real burnout is more specific and more serious. It's what happens when several batteries have been running on empty for too long without a real recharge. Burnout is more than exhaustion. It has three distinct signs: Pathfinder Tip The difference between running low and burned out is time. Running low happens to everyone. Burnout is what happens when you ignore running low long enough. The five batteries help you catch it early. Exhaustion Deep, lasting fatigue that a good night's sleep doesn't fix. You're tired before you start. Your physical and mental batteries are both critically low. Cynicism Detachment, or a "what's the point" feeling toward things that used to matter. Your spiritual battery is drained, and nothing feels meaningful anymore. Ineffectiveness The sense that nothing you do makes a difference. Your mental battery is so low that tasks you used to handle now feel impossible.

t: The Five Batteries: Running Low vs. Running Out
x: They don't work alone The five batteries affect each other. When your physical battery is critically low, your emotional battery drains faster. When your emotional battery is depleted, your mental battery can't perform at its best. When your spiritual battery runs empty, your social battery often follows. That's why "I just need to push through" is sometimes the wrong strategy. Pushing through doesn't recharge a drained battery. It just makes the crash harder when it comes. Pathfinder Tip You don't need all five batteries full to function well. You need to know which one is lowest, and do one small thing about it before it runs out. Worth saying clearly When your emotional or spiritual battery is truly empty, not just tired, that isn't a time management problem. It's a human problem, and it deserves real support. Your instructor, your Success Coach, and the OCTC Counseling Center are there for exactly these moments. Please use them.

t: The Five Batteries: Running Low vs. Running Out
x: Check in with yourself Reflect Right now, which battery is most depleted? What's draining it? Is there one battery you've been ignoring for a while, telling yourself you'll deal with it later? What's one small, realistic thing you could do in the next 24 hours to start recharging your lowest battery? Look ahead These questions are the heart of Question 2 in Mile Marker #3 . Time management gets all the attention, but the students who really find their way through college learn to read their own gauges. They know when they're running low and what they need, and they don't wait until they're completely empty to do something about it. That's self-knowledge, not weakness, and self-knowledge is one of the most professional things you can develop.

t: Divergent Minds: Your Brain, Your Way
x: Some brains work differently. That's not a flaw, but it does matter. Most time management advice assumes a particular kind of brain: one that starts tasks without much friction, stays focused with reasonable effort, tracks time naturally, and moves between activities without losing the thread. If that sounds like you, great. If it doesn't, if you've spent years wondering why the standard strategies don't work the way everyone says they should, this lesson is for you. It's also for everyone else. Understanding that brains work differently makes you a better student, a better teammate, and eventually a better colleague and leader. If you've ever been told you're lazy when you were trying harder than anyone knew… If you've ever started a task ten times without getting past the first line… If you've ever looked up and realized three hours had passed without you noticing, or felt like you'd been staring at something for three hours when it had only been ten minutes… If deadlines feel unreal until they're dangerously close… If you work brilliantly in some conditions and can barely function in others… This course sees you. And this lesson is specifically for you.

t: Divergent Minds: Your Brain, Your Way
x: What neurodivergence actually means Neurodivergence is an umbrella term for brains that process, learn, and function differently from what's considered neurotypical, the brain type most school and workplace systems were designed around. It includes ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia, anxiety disorders, sensory processing differences, and more. Some neurodivergent people have a formal diagnosis. Many don't, because they were never evaluated, because their differences were masked or compensated for, or because they're only now recognizing what's been true about them all along. You don't need a diagnosis for this lesson to apply to you. What neurodivergence is not is a measure of intelligence, ability, or potential. Some of the most capable people you'll ever meet have brains that work very differently from the standard model. Usually the challenge has less to do with what they can do than with places that weren't designed with their brains in mind. About this lesson This lesson isn't a diagnostic tool. It's meant to give you language for experiences you may have carried without a name, and strategies that work for a wider range of brains than the usual advice does.

t: Divergent Minds: Your Brain, Your Way
x: Executive function: the control center Most of the challenges neurodivergent students face in college come back to one thing: executive function . It's the set of mental skills that manage how you plan, start, organize, focus, handle emotions, and shift between tasks. Think of it as the brain's control center, or, to borrow from Lesson 3.3, the cockpit. For some brains, that system works less reliably because of how the brain is wired, not because of laziness or not caring. These challenges are real, common, and worth naming. Key Term Executive function: the mental skills you use to plan, start, organize, focus, manage emotions, and shift between tasks. Task initiation: starting is truly hard For many neurodivergent brains, starting a task, especially one that feels uncertain, boring, or overwhelming, takes far more effort than it looks like from the outside. This is real friction, not procrastination in the casual sense, and it can make the gap between "I need to do this" and "I'm doing this" feel impossible to close. What it looks like Sitting with an assignment open for an hour without producing anything Starting and restarting without getting traction Feeling frozen by a task you're fully capable of doing Needing a deadline crisis to get going, and then doing great work under pressure Time blindness: time feels different Many neurodivergent people, especially those with ADHD, experience time differently. There are really two times: now and not now . Future deadlines don't feel real until they become now. It's a difference in perception, not a choice, and it makes traditional planning advice unhelpful. What it looks like Deadlines that seemed far away suddenly arriving as emergencies Losing track of time completely when you're into something Regularly underestimating how long tasks take Time seeming to pass at different speeds depending on the situation Working memory: holding things in mind Working memory is your brain's ability to hold information for a moment while you use it, like a mental sticky note. When working memory is limited or unreliable, things slip: instructions get lost, multi-step tasks fall apart, and the thought you had two seconds ago is gone before you can use it. What it looks like Walking into a room and immediately forgetting why Losing your train of thought mid-sentence Reading a paragraph and retaining almost nothing Needing to write everything down, or it's gone Emotional regulation: feelings hit differently Many neurodivergent people feel emotions more intensely and have a harder time settling them quickly. Frustration, rejection, and overwhelm can hit hard and linger. It reflects a difference in how the brain processes and manages emotion, not immaturity. What it looks like A critical comment landing harder than it "should" Emotional reactions that feel bigger than the situation Having a hard time bouncing back after something goes wrong Avoiding tasks or situations that might bring frustration or failure Transitions: switching gears takes effort Moving from one task, place, or state of mind to another can take real effort for some brains. When you're deeply focused, sometimes called hyperfocus, switching away feels disruptive. And getting started on something new after a transition means rebuilding momentum from scratch. What it looks like Having trouble stopping a task even when you need to move on Needing extra time and energy to shift between subjects or places Feeling derailed after an interruption and struggling to get back on track Hyperfocusing on one thing at the expense of everything else

x: Strategies that work for more brains These strategies aren't only for neurodivergent students. They tend to work for a wider range of people than the standard advice does. Try what fits. Leave what doesn't. For task initiation Body doubling. Work near another person, even silently. Many brains get going more easily with someone else nearby: the library, a coffee shop, a study group that doesn't talk. The smallest possible start. Not "write the paper," but "open the document and type one sentence." Set the bar so low that starting is almost impossible to resist. Transition rituals. A specific song, a cup of something, a short walk before you sit down. It signals to your brain that work is starting. For time blindness Make time visible. Analog clocks, timers you can see, time-tracking apps. If time is invisible, your brain won't track it, so make it physical and present. Time anchors. Attach tasks to events instead of clock times. "After lunch, I'll do this" is more reliable than "at 1:00." Work backward from deadlines. If something is due Friday, when does it need to be done for that to happen? Set your own earlier deadline and make it real. For working memory Get it out of your head. Don't trust your brain to hold it. Write it down the moment it appears: checklists, voice memos, sticky notes, whatever you'll actually use. Close the loops. Unfinished tasks create mental background noise. When something is done, mark it done. When something can't be done now, write it down so your brain can let it go. One thing at a time. Single-tasking protects working memory. Every task switch costs more than you think. For emotional regulation Name it to tame it. Labeling an emotion, out loud or in writing, makes it less intense. "I'm frustrated" is easier to handle than a wave of something you can't name. Build in recovery time. After something emotionally hard, you may need more time than others to reset. Plan for it instead of fighting it. Know your triggers. What situations, times of day, or kinds of feedback reliably knock you off course? Knowing ahead of time lets you prepare instead of react. For transitions Warn yourself. Five minutes before a switch, acknowledge it's coming: "In five minutes, I'm switching to math." Sudden transitions are harder than prepared ones. Build buffers. Don't schedule tasks back to back. Give yourself time between classes, subjects, and places. Leave a breadcrumb. Before you stop working, write one sentence about where you left off and what comes next. Restarting gets much easier. For your environment Know what your brain needs. Silence or background noise? Movement or stillness? Natural light or controlled light? Experiment on purpose instead of defaulting to what you think you should need. Protect your best conditions. When you find a place where you work well, treat it like a resource: go back to it, and protect it. Simplify your setup. The more decisions you make before starting, the less energy you have for the work itself.

Key takeaways Professionalism is a pattern, not a performance. It's being someone people can count on, including owning it when things go wrong. Priorities first, schedule second. Name your Musts before you touch the calendar, and leave white space for real life. Protect your best hour. Put your most important work where your energy is highest, and put the phone out of reach. Finding, evaluating, and responsibly using information to make good decisions. 10 10 Essential Skills · #10 Information Literacy

What this skill is You're living in the most information-rich moment in human history, and one of the most information-polluted. More content is produced every day than anyone could take in over a lifetime. AI tools produce confident, detailed, believable answers in seconds. Social media shows you whatever is most engaging, not most accurate. News, opinion, marketing, and misinformation often look identical at first glance. Information Literacy is the skill that cuts through all of that. It means knowing how to ask the right questions, find credible sources, evaluate what you're reading, and use information responsibly to make real decisions, without doubting everything. It's one of the most transferable skills you'll build in college. It applies to every class, every job, and every decision you make as a citizen, consumer, and professional. Information is everywhere. The real question is whether it's trustworthy, and whether you can tell.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You can identify topics that call for information before you decide. You can use basic search strategies with familiar resources. You can name strengths and weaknesses of information sources. You can describe the main ideas from a variety of sources. You can identify where information came from. Milestone Your target You ask questions sized right for your field or situation. You use search strategies that find credible resources for your specific need. You analyze sources for bias, expertise, and point of view, not just surface credibility. You see connections between sources and use them to make well-informed decisions. You give appropriate credit to the sources you use. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from taking information in to actively questioning it, and using what you find with intention and integrity.
