What the research says, and what to do with it. Most students study the way they were taught to study, which often isn't how learning actually works. Rereading notes feels productive. Highlighting feels like engagement. Cramming the night before feels like urgency. None of these is especially effective, and the research on this is consistent. This lesson covers four strategies with strong evidence behind them. They aren't magic, and they don't work the same way for every brain. But understanding why they work helps you decide whether and how to use them in your own life. The goal is to study in ways that stick, not to study more.

Four strategies worth trying 1 Retrieval practice: test yourself before the test tests you The best-supported study strategy in learning research is also one of the least intuitive: testing yourself on material, before you feel ready, works better than reviewing it. Pulling information out of memory strengthens it in ways that rereading doesn't. Every time you struggle to recall something and then find the answer, you build a stronger memory than if you'd just read it again. That struggle is what makes it work. Close your notes. Write down everything you remember from class without looking. Then check what you missed. The gaps are what you need to study. Use flashcards, but try to recall the answer before you flip the card. Looking at both sides at once is review, not retrieval. After a reading, close the book and answer: what were the three most important things I just read? Try it and notice After your next class, spend five minutes writing down what you remember without looking at your notes. Notice what came easily and what didn't. That's your study list. Key Term Retrieval practice: studying by pulling information out of your memory, like quizzing yourself, instead of reading it again. 2 Spaced practice: come back before you forget Memory fades over time, and reviewing material just as it starts to fade works better than reviewing it right after you learn it. This is called the spacing effect , and it's why cramming gets you through tomorrow's test but not next month's. You don't need a complicated system. Study something, wait a day or two, and review it again. Wait a little longer, and review again. Each time you come back, the memory gets stronger and lasts longer. Spend 10 minutes on your notes the day of class. Come back two days later for another 10. Review again before the exam. Three short sessions beat one long one. Keep a running list of concepts you're shaky on. Revisit it every few days instead of waiting for exam week. Try it and notice Schedule one 10-minute review of this week's material for two days from now, and set a reminder. Notice whether you remember more or less than you expected, and what that tells you about how spacing works for your brain. Look back at Put your review sessions in My Week at a Glance . 3 Elaborative interrogation: ask why until it makes sense Elaborative interrogation means asking "why" and "how" as you study, and connecting new information to things you already know. Instead of memorizing facts, you build meaning, and meaning sticks better than isolated facts. This strategy tends to work especially well for students whose brains are drawn to patterns and connections, and less well for those who find open-ended questions hard to pin down. If that's you, pair it with retrieval practice. Reading about a historical event: don't just memorize the date. Ask why it happened when it did, and what would have had to be different for it not to happen. Studying a concept in biology: don't just memorize the definition. Ask why it works this way, and what would happen if it didn't. After reading anything, ask "So what?" Why does this matter? How does it connect to what I already know? Try it and notice Pick one concept from a current class. Write three "why" or "how" questions about it and try to answer them. Notice whether the concept feels clearer or more confusing afterward. Both are useful information. 4 Interleaving: mix it up on purpose Most students study one topic until it feels comfortable, then move to the next. That feels efficient, but research suggests that mixing different topics or problem types in one session leads to better long-term learning, even though it feels harder in the moment. That difficulty is part of why it works. When you have to figure out which approach fits which problem, your brain does more work, and that work builds understanding that lasts. Instead of doing 20 math problems of the same type in a row, do 5 of one type, then 5 of another, then come back to the first. It will feel harder, and that's a sign it's working. When reviewing for a test that covers several chapters, shuffle the topics instead of going in order. Try it and notice In your next study session for a class with several topics, switch between them every 15 to 20 minutes. Notice how it feels compared to sticking with one. Feeling unsure is normal. That's the learning happening.

What feels productive but isn't These are the study habits students rely on most, and why the research isn't kind to them. Feels productive Rereading notes or the textbook. It builds familiarity, not learning. You recognize the material, but recognizing isn't recalling. Instead Retrieval practice. Close the notes. Try to recall. Then check. The effort of recalling is what builds the memory. Feels productive Highlighting everything. It's passive and feels like engagement. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Instead Write questions in the margin. Next to the important parts, write a question. Later, try to answer it without looking. Feels productive Cramming the night before. It fades fast. You may pass the test and remember almost nothing two weeks later. Instead Spaced practice. Three 20-minute sessions over three days usually beat one 60-minute session the night before. None of these strategies works perfectly for every brain or every subject. When one doesn't work for you, that tells you something about how you learn. It doesn't mean the strategy failed. Try one, notice what happens, and adjust. Lookout: Ask Your Success Coach If you've changed how you study and a class still isn't going well, ask your instructor where you stand. Then talk with your Success Coach. Your coach can connect you with tutoring at the Teaching & Learning Center and with Accessibility Services. Your coach can also help you figure out whether you can still raise the grade, and if not, whether withdrawing makes sense. Withdrawing can affect your financial aid, so talk with your coach before you decide. Not sure who your coach is? Lesson 2.2 shows you how to find them.

S Specific. What exactly will you do? Name the strategy and the class. M Measurable. How will you know you did it? A number, a count, a checkmark. A Achievable. Is it realistic for your life right now, with your work, family, and energy? R Relevant. Why this habit? Which class or goal does it help? T Time-bound. When, and how often? Give it a schedule and an end point. Not SMART "I'm going to study more for biology." SMART "For the rest of the semester, I'll spend 10 minutes quizzing myself on my biology notes every Tuesday and Thursday after class, and check it off in my planner. I'll know it's working if I can answer most of my own questions before each exam." Key Term SMART goal: a goal that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound. s: Using AI as a study partner
x: Using AI as a study partner AI Literacy BE Critical AI tools can support the strategies in this lesson when you use them to think alongside you, not instead of you. For example: Retrieval practice: "Quiz me on [topic]. Ask me five questions and don't give me the answers until I try." Then ask yourself whether the questions match what you actually need to know. Elaborative interrogation: "Explain why [concept] works the way it does, in plain language." Ask follow-up questions until it makes sense, and check the explanation against your course materials. Spaced practice: "List the key points from [topic] so I can review them." Cover the list and try to recall the points before you read it. Finding gaps: "What are the most commonly misunderstood parts of [topic]?" Use the answer to test your own understanding, not to replace it. Where to draw the line: using AI to quiz yourself is studying. Using AI to write your notes, your summaries, or your assignment answers is not, because it skips the work that builds your ability. You'll feel the difference when you sit down for the exam.

Four moves for evaluating any information, including what AI tells you. Every day you run into dozens of pieces of information: articles, posts, search results, AI answers, videos, and claims from people you trust. Most of it looks credible, but some of it isn't, and the gap between "looks credible" and "is credible" has never been harder to spot. SIFT is a practical method for closing that gap. It was developed by information literacy researcher Mike Caulfield, and it gives you four moves you can make quickly, in the moment, before you believe, share, or act on something. It works on news articles, social media, and AI-generated content, which may be where it matters most right now. Before you start: consider this You ask an AI tool, "What are the best study strategies for college students?" The answer is detailed, confident, and well organized. It mentions "research" and uses phrases like "studies show" and "experts recommend." It sounds authoritative. It reads like something from a credible source. You take notes and plan to follow the advice. The problem: AI tools sound authoritative whether or not they're accurate. There may be no actual study behind "studies show." The "expert" may not exist. The advice may be useful, or it may be a believable mix of things the AI was trained on. Without checking, you can't tell which. That's what SIFT is for.

The four moves S Stop Before you read the article, stop . Before you share the video, stop . Before you act on a strong reaction to a headline or a convincing AI summary, stop . This is the hardest move, because the information around you is designed to keep you moving. Headlines are written to provoke a reaction. AI answers are formatted to feel complete and final. Social media rewards the fast share. Stopping means pausing before your first reaction becomes your conclusion, not doubting everything. Ask yourself: Do I know this source? Do I know its reputation? Am I reacting to how confident this sounds instead of whether it's accurate? Applied to AI When an AI answer sounds complete and authoritative, stop. That confidence comes from how AI writes, not from evidence that the content is right, so pause before you use it. Watch: Stop, with Mike Caulfield (YouTube) I Investigate the source Before you read deeply, take a minute to find out what you're reading. Who made this? What's their purpose? What's the reputation of this person or organization? You're looking for context before you invest your attention, not reasons to dismiss it. The key technique is lateral reading : instead of reading deeper into the source itself, open a new tab and search for what others say about it. Professional fact-checkers work this way, and it's far more effective than judging credibility from the inside. Search the name of the publication, website, or author along with words like "bias," "credibility," or "fact-check." Check Wikipedia for background on news organizations, think tanks, or advocacy groups, as a quick starting point, not a final authority. Look at the "About" page, but don't stop there. Anyone can write an impressive About page. Applied to AI You can't look up an AI's reputation, but you can check its claims. If an AI answer names a specific study, expert, or statistic, investigate that claim directly. Does the study exist? Does the expert? Where does the number come from? Watch: Investigate the Source, with Mike Caulfield (YouTube) Key Term Lateral reading: checking a source by leaving it and searching what other sources say about it. Pathfinder Tip Lateral reading takes less than two minutes and catches things deep reading misses. Open a new tab before you commit to a source. It's the single most effective habit in the whole method. F Find better coverage Sometimes the best move is to stop judging the source you have and find a better source for the same information. If a claim matters enough to act on, it's worth seeing whether other credible sources report it the same way. Look for sources with a track record of accuracy, not sources that agree with you, and see how they handle the same claim. Search the specific claim, not the source, and see what several outlets say. For viral claims, use fact-checking sites like Snopes , PolitiFact , or AP Fact Check . For academic topics, search the OCTC Library databases for peer-reviewed sources on the same question. When several independent, credible sources report a claim the same way, that means something. Applied to AI When AI gives you information you plan to use for an assignment or a decision, find better coverage from a credible source before you rely on it. The AI answer is a starting point, not a destination. Watch: Find Better Coverage, with Mike Caulfield (YouTube) T Trace claims, quotes, and media to the original A lot of misinformation starts with something real, taken out of context: a real statistic used to support a false conclusion, a real quote trimmed to mean something the speaker didn't say, a real study cited for a finding it never showed. Tracing means following a claim back to where it started and asking: does the original actually say what this source claims it says? Click through links. Don't assume a linked source says what the article claims. When a statistic is cited, find the original study or report, not just the article about it. When a quote is used, find the full quote in its original setting. Speeches, interviews, and documents are usually findable. For images or videos, use a reverse image search to find where they first appeared. Applied to AI AI tools sometimes produce citations that look real but don't exist. This is called a hallucination . If an AI answer cites a source, trace it. If you can't find it, don't use it. If you find it and it says something different from what the AI claimed, that's your answer. Watch: Trace Claims, with Mike Caulfield (YouTube) Pathfinder Tip Most misinformation uses real information in misleading ways rather than telling an outright lie. Tracing takes longer than the other moves, but it's the one that finds the biggest problems.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
x: Did you cross the line, and did you notice? This happens to almost everyone, often without them noticing. A student starts a paper by asking AI for a few topic ideas. That feels reasonable. Brainstorming is exactly what AI is good for. Then they ask for an outline. Still feels fine. Then they're stuck on the introduction, so they ask AI to write a sample one "just to see what it might look like." It sounds pretty good, so parts of it end up in the draft. Later, worried the writing isn't polished enough, they ask AI to improve a paragraph. Then to make it sound more professional. Then to rewrite the conclusion. By the time the paper is done, they honestly can't say how much of it is theirs and how much came from AI. They weren't trying to cheat. The line moved one small step at a time, and nobody was keeping track of where it ended up. This is AI creep : AI's role in your work growing a little at a time, where each step feels small and reasonable, but the end result is very different from where you started. Key Term AI creep: the gradual, often unnoticed growth of AI's role in your work.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
x: The AI Creep Meter Each stage on this scale means AI plays a bigger role in producing the actual content of your work. The AI Creep Meter Brainstorming Outlining Drafting Revising Rewriting Submitting Lower stakes Higher stakes The farther AI moves into the creation of your work, the more important transparency becomes. Brainstorming and outlining are usually lower stakes. You're still doing the thinking, and AI is helping you organize it. As AI moves into drafting, revising, and rewriting, it does more of the work for you, and the line between "my work" and "AI's work" gets harder to see. That doesn't mean the right side of the meter is always off-limits. That depends on the assignment and your instructor. It means the farther right you go, the more important it is that you can explain what happened, and that you chose to go there on purpose. Look back at Lesson 1.4 : each assignment's AI use label tells you how far along the meter you're allowed to go.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
s: Set your boundary before you start
x: Set your boundary before you start The fix is deciding, before you open the chat, what role AI is allowed to play in this piece of work. Tools have jobs. A hammer is great for nails and useless for screws. AI is the same: useful for some jobs on a given assignment, the wrong tool for others. Before you start, ask yourself: What am I trying to learn from this assignment? What parts of this work need to be mine, in my own words and my own thinking? What role, if any, should AI play here? Then tell the AI that role directly. A few examples: Tutor Explain this concept in simple terms, but don't complete the assignment for me. Brainstorming partner Help me generate ideas and questions to explore. Don't write content I can submit. Study coach Ask me questions that help me think this through myself. Editor Give me feedback on clarity and organization, but don't rewrite my work. Setting the boundary up front does two things: it keeps AI in its lane, and it gives you something to point back to if you're asked how you used it.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
s: Why this connects to BE Honest
x: Why this connects to BE Honest AI Literacy BE Honest BE Honest is less about getting caught than about whether your work is worthy of your name. AI creep makes that question hard to answer, even when you aren't hiding anything, because you've lost track yourself. If an instructor asked you right now, "How did you use AI on this?", could you answer clearly? If the honest answer is "I'm not totally sure," notice that, because it tells you the boundary slipped.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
x: What attribution actually looks like "Be transparent about AI use" can feel vague until you see it written out. Attribution doesn't need to be long or formal. It needs to be specific enough that someone else could tell what AI did and didn't do. Less creep, clearly credited "I used AI to brainstorm three possible topics and to help me build an outline. The writing, examples, and conclusions are my own." More creep, still credited "I drafted this myself, then used AI to revise my conclusion paragraph for clarity. I reviewed the changes and adjusted the wording so it still sounds like me." Both examples name what AI did (brainstorm, outline, revise one paragraph), and both are specific enough that the student could explain more if asked. Neither says "I used AI" and stops there. A vague disclosure is hard to act on, for you or your instructor. A quick way to write your own: name the stage or stages on the Creep Meter where AI was involved, then say what stayed yours. Look back at Keep a trail in Lesson 1.4 makes attribution much easier.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
x: Before you submit, ask yourself Can I explain my work and how AI helped me? (That's the third of the 3 Qs .) Could I show my process if asked? Does this still show my own learning and thinking? Would I be comfortable talking through my AI use with my instructor? If any answer is no, that's the moment to pause, not after you've submitted.

t: AI Literacy: Beware of the Creep
x: In your own life Reflect Think of a time you used AI for a task, for school or anything else. Where would that use land on the AI Creep Meter? Has your AI use ever gone further than you planned, without you really deciding it should? What did that feel like once you noticed? What would it look like to set a boundary with AI before your next assignment, and tell the AI what that boundary is? Look ahead The first question here is Question 4 in Mile Marker #4 . AI policies are still evolving, and they'll keep changing. Being transparent, being honest, and owning your learning stay in your hands, whatever the policy says. The most important decision about AI use is the boundary you set at the beginning of a project, not anything you do at the end.

Technology made recording easy. That doesn't make it automatic. A few years ago, recording a class took equipment. Now it takes one tap on a phone. AI note-taking apps can join an online class, transcribe everything, and summarize the discussion before you've closed your laptop. The technology is impressive, and the questions it raises are real. KCTCS doesn't have one system-wide recording policy. That means the rules vary by instructor, by course, and by situation, and your judgment, your professionalism, and your respect for the people in the room matter more than a rulebook. This lesson is about building that judgment.

s: Three principles to guide your decisions
x: Three principles to guide your decisions 1 Respect the course: check the syllabus, and ask Your syllabus is the contract for each course. Some instructors allow recording for personal study. Some don't allow it at all. Many don't mention it, and silence is not the same as permission. The professional move, every time, is to ask before you record, not after you've already started. Check your syllabus first. The answer may already be there. If it isn't, ask your instructor directly, before class or by email. If an instructor says no, that's the answer. It isn't a negotiation. Permission in one class doesn't carry over to another. Ask each instructor. How to ask: a simple script "Professor [Name], I sometimes have trouble capturing everything during lectures, and recordings help me review. Do you allow students to record class for personal study?" The request is specific, professional, and honest about your reason. Most instructors appreciate being asked rather than finding out later that they were recorded. Pathfinder Tip If recording is part of a documented accommodation, work through Accessibility Services to get it in writing. An official accommodation is different from informal permission, and it protects you. 2 Respect the people: your classmates and your instructor A classroom is a shared space. When you record, you capture more than the instructor's voice. You capture your classmates' questions, comments, and discussion, and they didn't agree to be recorded. This matters more than most students realize. A classmate who shares something personal, asks a question they feel unsure about, or says something they'd like to take back has a reasonable expectation that it stays in the room. An instructor's lectures may be their intellectual property. Sharing recordings without permission can be a serious violation. Recording classmates without their knowledge or consent raises real privacy concerns, even when it's technically easy. Posting or sharing recordings anywhere outside the class, like social media or group chats, is almost always inappropriate and may violate College policy. Even with permission, treat a recording as personal study material, not content to share. Pathfinder Tip The test is simple: would the people being recorded be comfortable knowing it, and knowing how the recording will be used? If the answer is anything but a clear yes, don't record, or ask first. 3 Respect your own learning: recording isn't learning There's a real risk that recording replaces paying attention instead of supporting it. When you know a recording exists, your brain tends to relax, because "it's captured." But captured audio isn't understanding. Making sense of the material still takes work, and that work happens in real time, not during playback. Students who rely heavily on recordings often end up with hours of audio they never revisit. Taking notes as you go, even imperfect ones, helps you remember more than recording alone. If you record, use it alongside your notes, not instead of them. Go back to specific moments you marked as unclear. Don't relisten to the whole thing. Working to keep up in real time is part of learning. Don't hand that work off entirely. Pathfinder Tip If you're recording because you can't keep up, pay attention to that. Talk to your instructor, and ask the Teaching & Learning Center about note-taking strategies. The recording may be covering a gap worth addressing directly.

AI note-takers: a separate conversation AI Literacy BE Safe BE Honest BE Responsible Tools like Otter.ai, Fireflies, and similar apps go beyond basic recording. They upload audio to another company's servers, process it with outside AI systems, and store transcripts in ways you may not fully control. Before you use any AI note-taker in a class or meeting, think through these questions: Who has the data? Uploading a recording sends your classmates' voices and your instructor's lecture to a company's servers. Read the privacy policy before you use it. Did everyone agree? Your classmates didn't sign up to have their voices processed by an AI company. That's a real privacy concern, not a technicality. Does your instructor know what the tool does? Many instructors don't realize that "I'm using an AI note-taker" means their lecture goes to an outside platform. That's a different conversation from asking to record on your phone. Is the transcript accurate? AI transcription makes mistakes, some small, some serious. One misheard term or date can send you studying the wrong thing. Check it against your course materials. Are you still paying attention? The same risk as recording applies here, maybe more. If the app is "handling it," your brain may check out completely. The responsible move: treat an AI note-taker like any recording device. Ask permission, be upfront about what the tool does, and use what it produces with a critical eye. If an instructor allows recording but hasn't thought about AI note-takers, have that conversation specifically.

You already have powerful tools. Here's how to use them for school. As a KCTCS student, you have free access to the full Microsoft Office 365 suite, including tools that go well beyond Word and PowerPoint. This Trail Tip covers the ones most useful for school: OneNote for organizing your course life, OneDrive for keeping your files safe and easy to reach, Teams for group work, and Microsoft Copilot as a study support tool. You don't need to master them. Knowing they exist lets you reach for the right one when you need it. Look back at Module 1 Trail Tip: Your Free Microsoft Office 365 Access shows how to get the apps.

s: OneNote: your digital Trapper Keeper Start here
x: OneNote: your digital Trapper Keeper Start here OneNote is a free-form digital notebook organized into notebooks, sections, and pages. Think of it as a Trapper Keeper that lives in the cloud: you can open it on any device, it never gets left at home, and you can't lose pages because you forgot to put them back. Unlike a Word document, OneNote isn't linear. You can type anywhere on the page, add images, paste links, record audio, and draw diagrams, and organize it all the way your brain works, not the way a template tells you to. How to use it for school One notebook per semester. Make a section for each class, then a page for each lecture or topic, so everything is in one place. Capture anything. Paste a screenshot of a slide, type your notes next to it, and add a question you want to follow up on. No formatting required. Search everything. OneNote searches all of your notes. If you wrote it down, you can find it. Share with study partners. Share a section with a classmate to take notes together without sending files back and forth. Come back and add to it. Revisit old notes, add new thoughts, and mark what mattered. Your notes become a living document. Pathfinder Tip Set up a "Class Notes" notebook before your first class of the semester, with one section per course. Five minutes of setup pays off every week.

Thinking clearly with numbers, which you already do every day. 3 10 Essential Skills · #3 Quantitative Reasoning

First, let's name the thing If your stomach dropped a little when you read "Quantitative Reasoning," you're not alone. A lot of people carry math anxiety from years of feeling like numbers weren't for them. Maybe a teacher made you feel slow. Maybe a test went badly. Maybe at some point you decided you were a "words person, not a numbers person." Quantitative Reasoning, as Kentucky defines it, has little to do with solving equations or memorizing formulas. It means using numbers to understand the world around you and to make better decisions. You already do that, probably without noticing. Quantitative Reasoning is thinking with numbers, and you already do it.

You already do this Every time you work with numbers in a real situation, outside of a test, you're practicing Quantitative Reasoning. At the gas station "Gas is $3.49 a gallon and I need about half a tank, so roughly $25." That's estimating with real data. Checking your grade "I have an 82, and there's one more assignment worth 20%. What do I need to pass?" That's percentages applied to a real decision. Reading a paycheck "I worked 23 hours at $12.50. Why does my check say $215?" That's understanding taxes, deductions, and gross versus take-home pay. Tracking spending "I spent $180 on food this week, and my food budget is $200 a month. That's already 90% gone." That's using numbers to describe what's happening. Reading the news "The article says crime is up 40%. But 40% of what? Starting from how many?" That's questioning the assumptions behind data. Making a decision "Is it cheaper to drive or take a rideshare? Let me actually figure out the cost." That's using numbers to choose the best option.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You can pick out key information from graphs, tables, and equations. You can do basic arithmetic and calculate percentages and simple statistics. You can tell when numbers are relevant to a problem. Milestone Your target You show real-life data in ways that make its meaning clear, not just read it. You use percentages and statistics to describe what's actually happening in a real situation. You use numbers to state your assumptions and work through problems: not just calculating, but reasoning. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from working with numbers to thinking with them: from calculating to reasoning.

s: Where it shows up in this module
x: Where it shows up in this module Module 5 is where Quantitative Reasoning gets personal. Every part of it works with numbers in a real setting: your spending, your patterns, your decisions. The Dollar Tracker. Recording what you actually spent, by category, over time, turns numbers into a picture of your real life. Reading your spending patterns. Noticing "food delivery is about 30% of what I spend" is using statistics to describe what's really happening. The Budget Builder. Giving every dollar a job until nothing is left is reasoning with numbers to make a plan, and checking that it adds up. Questioning the data. When a statistic sounds surprising, like "the average student spends $X on food," asking "compared to what? Which students?" is Quantitative Reasoning. Numbers only mean something in context.

A note on math anxiety If numbers have felt threatening in the past, you're allowed to say so. Math anxiety is real, it's common, and it doesn't mean you can't build this skill. It usually means something went wrong in how you were taught, not that you're incapable. Quantitative Reasoning at this level doesn't require algebra or calculus. It takes attention, honesty, and a willingness to look at numbers without flinching. You have all of those. Pathfinder Tip If a number task makes the anxiety kick in, pause, breathe, and ask: "What is this number actually telling me?" That question is the heart of the skill.

In your own life Reflect Think of a recent decision that involved numbers, even a small one. What information did you use? What did you estimate or calculate? Is there a number in your life right now, like a bill, a grade, or a balance, that you've been avoiding? What would it take to look at it honestly? When you hear a statistic in the news or on social media, what's your first instinct: believe it, question it, or ignore it? What would Quantitative Reasoning tell you to do? Skill definition and Milestone indicators are based on the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education's Kentucky Graduate Profile .

A feeling of steadiness you can work toward from wherever you're starting. Money touches everything: your stress level, your schedule, your ability to say yes to an opportunity or no to something that doesn't work for you. When your financial life feels out of control, even a little, it creates a low hum of anxiety under everything else you're trying to do. Financial wellness doesn't depend on having a certain amount of money. It comes from having enough awareness and intention around money that you feel steady, or at least less reactive. You can work toward that no matter what's in your bank account right now. Financial wellness is a direction, not a destination. Key Term Financial wellness: feeling steady and in some control of your money, because you know where it goes and make choices on purpose.

s: What financial wellness is, and isn't
x: What financial wellness is, and isn't The term gets used a lot of different ways, so it helps to be clear about what it is and isn't. Financial wellness is Knowing roughly where your money goes Feeling some control, even if it's limited Handling a small unexpected expense without a crisis Making intentional choices about money, even small ones Knowing what resources are available to you Worrying less about money over time Financial wellness isn't Having a lot of money Never struggling financially Following a perfect budget every month Having no debt Saving a fixed percentage of every paycheck Doing everything "right" by someone else's standard If money is tight right now, because you're supporting family, managing debt, or working more than one job, financial wellness still applies to you. It just looks different at different income levels. The goal is to feel more in control of your own picture, not to match someone else's.

Money stress and school Financial stress is one of the biggest, and least talked about, barriers to finishing college. It's uncomfortable, and it's also mentally expensive. When you're worried about money, your brain keeps working on that problem in the background, even when you're trying to focus on something else. Research consistently links financial stress to trouble with concentration, memory, decision-making, and planning ahead, which are exactly the skills college asks for. Students under financial stress are more likely to cut back their classes, step away, or leave college entirely. They could do the work, but the weight of money worries made it hard to focus on anything else. That's a real mental load, not a character flaw, and it deserves to be taken seriously. You can't manage what you can't see. Awareness comes first. Most people think they know where their money goes, until they actually look. College makes spending even harder to track: gas, groceries, random fees, subscriptions you forgot you had, late-night delivery, "just one thing" from the store. It adds up faster than it should, and usually in ways you didn't see coming. This lesson won't judge your spending. It will help you see it clearly, and then give your money a plan. Clarity is the real starting point for any financial decision, at any income, in any life situation. Before you fix anything, you need to see it clearly.

Why this matters, for everyone Money stress shows up differently depending on where you're starting. I live with my parents and have some money from work, but I never know where it goes by the end of the month. I'm working full-time, paying rent, and trying to make it all stretch. I have financial aid money right now, but I know it won't last the whole semester. I'm supporting my family. There's not much wiggle room, and I'm stressed about it constantly. All four of those students could be in this course, and all four benefit from the same first move: knowing what's actually happening with their money before trying to change it.

Three steps to seeing clearly 1 Look at the last week or two You don't need bank statements, though you can use them if you have them. Start by asking: where did my money go in the last week or two? Rough estimates are fine. You want a general picture, not an audit. Common student spending categories: Food: groceries, snacks, eating out, delivery Transportation: gas, rideshare, parking School: textbooks, supplies, fees, printing Subscriptions: streaming, music, apps, cloud storage Personal: toiletries, clothing, household Social: going out, gifts, splitting bills Bills: phone, rent, utilities, insurance Random: convenience stores, online orders, impulse buys Pathfinder Tip Use the Dollar Tracker to make this concrete. Option A looks back at the past week. Option B tracks the next week as it happens. Pick the one that fits where you are. 2 Notice what surprises you Most people find at least one thing they didn't expect, and that surprise is where awareness starts doing its work. "I eat out way more than I thought." "Small purchases, $5 here and $8 there, add up to a lot." "I didn't plan for school fees until they hit." You don't have to fix anything yet. Noticing is worth more than it sounds. 3 Find your money leaks A money leak is spending that doesn't line up with what you actually value or need. What counts is spending you recognize as out of line with your own priorities, not spending someone else thinks is unnecessary. Delivery fees when you already have food at home Subscriptions you forgot about and don't use Convenience buys that happen because you didn't plan ahead Impulse buys you regret within a day or two Social spending that felt like an obligation instead of a choice Pathfinder Tip A money leak isn't the same as spending on something you enjoy. If eating out truly matters to you, that's a priority, not a leak. The leak is spending that leaves you wondering where your money went.

Give every dollar a job Once you know where your money goes, you can decide where it should go. The approach that works best for most students is a zero-based budget : when money comes in, you give every dollar a job until there are zero dollars left without one. Zero doesn't mean you spend it all. Savings, paying down debt, and fun are all jobs too. The difference is that you decide on purpose, when the money arrives, instead of trying to figure out at the end of the month what happened. Key Term Zero-based budget: a plan that gives every dollar coming in a job (spending, saving, or paying debt) until money in minus money assigned equals zero. List what's coming in this month Paychecks, financial aid, help from family, anything else. If your income changes, plan on the lowest amount you can count on. If a financial aid refund has to last the whole semester, divide it across the months it needs to cover. List every place it needs to go Start with your Musts: housing, food, getting to school and work, bills. Then the rest: savings, school costs, personal, fun. Assign until you reach $0 Give each category an amount until money in minus money assigned equals zero. If you run out before you run out of categories, trim something. If money is left over, give it a job, even if the job is savings. Adjust as the month happens Real life will change the plan. When you overspend in one category, move money from another. That's how the budget is supposed to work. Example: one student's zero-based month Coming in Amount Paychecks (part-time job) $1,400 Help from family $200 Total coming in $1,600 Every dollar's job Amount Share of rent $550 Groceries $260 Gas and car $180 Utilities and phone $120 Car insurance $110 Fun and social $90 Emergency fund $80 Personal and household $70 School costs $60 Giving or family $40 Subscriptions $40 Total assigned $1,600 $1,600 coming in − $1,600 assigned = $0 left to assign . Every dollar has a job. Try it: the Budget Builder Build your own zero-based budget for one month. It adds up as you type and shows what's left to assign. Real, rounded, or practice numbers all work, and nothing you type leaves your device. Open the Budget Builder

The presentation, the steps to get and keep your aid, and who to ask. Financial aid is money to help you pay for college. It's worth knowing how it works, because it can change what you can afford and how many classes you can take. This Trail Tip gathers OCTC's financial aid information in one place: the presentation from the Financial Aid office, the steps to get and keep your aid, and where to go with questions.

Getting and keeping your aid These steps follow OCTC's Financial Aid Checklist. If you've already done some of them, start where you are. Create your StudentAid.gov account This account, also called an FSA ID, is how you sign in to the FAFSA and sign it. s: Two numbers that protect your aid
x: Two numbers that protect your aid To keep getting financial aid, you have to show you're making progress toward your credential. Colleges call this Satisfactory Academic Progress , or SAP. It's checked at the end of every semester, and two numbers cause most of the trouble. Your GPA: 2.0 or higher Your cumulative GPA, which covers all your classes so far, has to stay at 2.0 or above. That's a C average. Your completion rate: 67% or higher You have to pass at least two-thirds of the credit hours you sign up for. If you sign up for 12 credit hours and pass 6, your rate is 50%. Key term Completion rate : the credit hours you've passed, divided by the credit hours you've attempted. Look back at How your GPA is calculated A W still counts against you A class you withdraw from (W), fail (E), or leave incomplete (I) counts as attempted but not passed. A W doesn't lower your GPA, but it does lower your completion rate. Withdrawing from two classes in one semester can be enough to put your aid at risk. There's also a limit on total credit hours: aid covers up to 150% of the credits your program requires. Changing programs several times or repeating many classes can use that up. If you fall below The first time, you're placed on warning and can still receive aid for one more semester. If you're still below after that, your aid is suspended. You can appeal a suspension through Student Self-Service, and Financial Aid can explain how. Notices about your status go to your KCTCS email shortly after the semester ends, so keep checking it over the break. KCTCS Satisfactory Academic Progress policy : the full rules, including warning, suspension, and appeals Satisfactory Academic Progress at OCTC : OCTC's summary and how to appeal

Turning what you know into real decisions. 9 10 Essential Skills · #9 Knowledge Application

What this skill is Knowing things is the starting point. Knowledge Application is using what you know to make real decisions. Knowledge Application is the bridge between learning and doing. Knowing your interests, your strengths, and what programs exist at OCTC is a start. The skill is connecting that knowledge to real decisions about your academic path, your career direction, and your life, in ways that are thoughtful, specific, and honest about your actual situation. It may be the most important skill in college, because it's the one that makes everything else useful. Without it, you collect information but don't go anywhere with it. With it, what you learn becomes a tool for moving forward. Knowledge Application turns "I know that" into "I did something with it."

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You can name the kind of work you're interested in and how it connects to career opportunities. You can describe the basic knowledge, skills, and abilities your career direction requires. You explore careers with your strengths, interests, values, and goals in mind. Milestone Your target You use what you've learned to solve basic problems related to your career path. You can explain the ideas behind putting knowledge, skills, and abilities to work in your field. You reflect on your experiences to judge how well a career fits you, and can explain your reasons. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from exploring possibilities to making informed, reasoned choices, and being able to explain why.

t: Explore Your Interests with Career Coach
s: What it measures: the six interest types
x: What it measures: the six interest types Career Coach uses the RIASEC model, a widely used framework developed by psychologist John Holland, to sort interests into six types. Most people have a mix of two or three strong types. Knowing your mix helps you see which work environments and career directions tend to fit people like you. Key Term RIASEC: six interest types (Realistic, Investigative, Artistic, Social, Enterprising, Conventional) used to match people with work they're likely to enjoy. R Realistic Doers who like working with their hands, tools, machines, or the outdoors. Practical and results-focused. I Investigative Thinkers who love working through problems, research, and ideas. Curious and analytical. A Artistic Creators who value self-expression, imagination, and freedom. Drawn to design, writing, and music. S Social Helpers who enjoy working with and for people. Drawn to education, healthcare, and community work. E Enterprising Leaders who like persuading and driving results. Drawn to business, sales, and management. C Conventional Organizers who thrive with structure and systems. Detail-focused, drawn to data, finance, and process. Your top two or three types together tell a more useful story than any one type alone. A Social-Investigative mix points somewhere different than a Social-Enterprising one, even though both include Social. Pay attention to the combination, not only the highest score.

How credentials stack, and how your results connect to real programs. Picking a program means choosing a credential, a timeline, and a direction, along with a subject you like. Those choices shape what you take, when you can finish, and where you can go next. Most students never get a clear explanation of how this works before they register for their first class. This lesson fixes that: how credentials stack at OCTC, how your Career Coach results connect to programs, and what to bring to your Success Coach.

How credentials stack At OCTC, many credentials are designed to build on each other. Courses are packaged into certificates, certificates can stack into diplomas, and diplomas can stack into degrees. Transfer degrees lead to four-year universities. You don't always have to start at the bottom, and you don't have to stop at the top. Key Term Stackable credential: a credential whose courses also count toward the next, bigger credential. How credentials build on each other Courses Individual classes, packaged into credentials Certificate A focused set of courses around one skill area. The shortest path to a credential. Diploma Deeper than a certificate, often technical or career-focused AAS degree Associate in Applied Science The full career-ready degree for technical and professional programs Or take a different path: AA or AS degree Associate in Arts or Associate in Science Designed to transfer to a four-year university Certificate, diploma, AAS: toward the workforce AA, AS: toward a four-year university

What each credential means Credit hours and length vary by program, so check the specific program in the KCTCS catalog . Certificate The fastest path to a specific skill or entry-level credential Often stackable: the credits count toward a diploma or AAS Good for getting into the workforce quickly or adding a skill Some can be finished in a semester or two Diploma More in-depth preparation than a certificate Common in technical and health programs Credits often apply toward an AAS if you keep going Usually about one to two years of full-time study AAS degree The full career-ready credential for technical and professional programs Usually about two years of full-time study Includes general education courses alongside your major courses Some programs have transfer agreements. Ask your Success Coach. AA or AS degree Designed to transfer to Kentucky's four-year universities Associate in Arts (AA) for humanities, social sciences, and similar fields Associate in Science (AS) for science and math fields Built to count toward a bachelor's degree, protecting the work you've already done An AAS isn't a dead end. It's designed for the workforce, and many AAS graduates go on to a four-year university by taking additional general education courses, and some universities have agreements with KCTCS colleges that make the path clearer. If you might want a bachelor's degree someday, ask your Success Coach about transfer options before you assume it isn't possible. Pathfinder Tip In a technical program, ask your advisor: "Does this certificate stack toward a diploma or AAS?" You may be closer to the next credential than you think, and able to earn something with job value before you finish.

s: Think like a strategist, not just a scheduler
x: Think like a strategist, not just a scheduler Most students treat registration like a puzzle: find classes that don't overlap with work and family. That's necessary, but strategic planning asks a few more questions before you open the schedule. 1 Know what has to happen first Most programs have prerequisites , courses you must finish before you can take the next one. In some programs, getting the order wrong costs a whole semester. In others, missing an application or entrance exam deadline can push your start back a full year. Math prerequisites are the most common bottleneck. Many health, science, and business programs need college-level math before you can move ahead. Find out what math your program requires, and when. Application deadlines exist for competitive programs, like many health programs. Missing one can mean waiting a year to start. Entrance exams. Some programs require an entrance exam that takes time to prepare for and schedule. Nursing programs, for example, often use one. Find out now, not after two semesters of prerequisites. Key Term Prerequisite: a course you must finish before you're allowed to take another course. Pathfinder Tip Ask your Success Coach: "Are there any deadlines, entrance exams, or application windows I need to know about for this program?" That one question can save you a semester or more. 2 Be realistic about your load Full-time is usually 12 credit hours a semester, but 12 isn't right for everyone. Students who work full time, care for family, or are coming back after time away often find that a lighter load done well serves them better than a full load done poorly. A rough rule: for every credit hour, expect 2 to 3 hours of work outside class each week. A 12-credit load can mean 24 to 36 hours of studying on top of class time. Your first semesters are for learning how college works for you: what your time really looks like and how demanding your courses are. Starting lighter and doing well is a stronger foundation than overloading and struggling. Part-time is a real option. It takes longer, but finishing at your own pace beats not finishing at all. Pathfinder Tip Financial aid often requires a minimum number of credit hours. Before you choose a lighter semester, check with Financial Aid about what keeps your aid in place. Look back at Your time log from Module 3 shows how many hours you really have. 3 Look more than one semester ahead You don't need a perfect multi-year plan. But looking past next semester, even roughly, shows whether you're on track, whether your prerequisites will be done in time, and whether your finish date is realistic. The Academic Planner gives you room for next semester and two more. Start with next semester. Looking ahead, even imperfectly, is what matters. Pathfinder Tip Not every course is offered every semester. Some are offered only once a year. Missing one can delay you significantly, so ask your advisor which courses have limited offerings. 4 Keep it flexible Life happens and programs change. You might discover you dislike something you thought you'd love, or love something you didn't expect. A good plan absorbs change without falling apart. General education courses often count toward several programs. Taking them early protects you if you change direction. A certificate in one area doesn't lock you out of another program. Stackable credentials let you pivot without starting over. Review your plan with your advisor every semester, not only once.

What strategic planning looks like The same thinking plays out differently depending on where you're headed. Interested in nursing Nursing programs typically have a competitive application with a deadline, prerequisite courses in areas like anatomy and math, and often an entrance exam. Strategic move: Find out the application timeline now and work backward to plan your prerequisites. Planning to transfer Transfer works best when you know your likely university and major, since schools differ in what they accept for a given major. Strategic move: Name one or two universities you're considering, and ask your advisor which courses fit their requirements. Exploring a technical program Many technical programs, like welding, HVAC, and automotive, offer certificates that stack into diplomas and AAS degrees. Strategic move: Map the full credential ladder so you earn something meaningful at each step, not just at the end. Still deciding You're not stuck. General education courses like English, math, and social sciences are required in almost every program and transfer widely. Strategic move: Start with general education while you explore. It builds a foundation that works wherever you land.

t: Wait... How Is My Grade Actually Calculated?
x: Most students don't know. Now you will. At some point, you're going to check your grade and feel confused because the number doesn't match what you expected. You'll wonder what's being counted, how much each assignment matters, and whether you can still turn things around. This Trail Tip answers those questions before you need them. There are two things to understand: how your grade works inside a single class, and how that grade feeds into your overall GPA. Both are simpler than they look, once someone explains them.

t: Wait... How Is My Grade Actually Calculated?
s: How your grade works in a class
x: How your grade works in a class Most courses use one of two grading approaches. Knowing which one your instructor uses changes how you think about every assignment. Points-based grading Every assignment is worth a set number of points. Your grade is your total earned points divided by the total possible points. Assignment Earned Possible Reflection 1 4 4 Reflection 2 3 4 Discussion 1 1 Quick check 0.5 1 Total 8.5 10 8.5 ÷ 10 = 85%, a B Weighted grading Different categories of work count for different percentages of your grade. How you do in each category matters more than the points on any single assignment. Category Weight Your score Counts as Exams 50% 78% 39.0 Assignments 30% 92% 27.6 Participation 20% 85% 17.0 Final grade 83.6% 39.0 + 27.6 + 17.0 = 83.6%, a B In weighted grading, a strong exam score matters more than a perfect homework record. Which one does your course use? Check each course's syllabus. It tells you whether the course is points-based or weighted, and how the work breaks down. Your syllabus is the contract for the course, so it's the place to look first, including for this one. Don't fall into this trap It's easy to look at a small assignment and think, "That's basically nothing." But small assignments add up. A handful of low-point activities can make up a real share of your final grade, and skipping them is one of the most common ways a B turns into a C. There are no throwaway assignments.

t: Wait... How Is My Grade Actually Calculated?
s: How your class grade feeds your GPA
x: How your class grade feeds your GPA Your GPA, or grade point average, summarizes your academic performance across all your courses, and it's simple math once you see how it works. Key Term Quality points: a course's grade points multiplied by its credit hours. 1 Know the grade scale Letter grades convert to grade points on a 4.0 scale. A 4.0 B 3.0 C 2.0 D 1.0 E 0.0 At KCTCS colleges, the failing grade is an E , not an F. That's because F has its own job: it's used only in pass-fail courses, where you earn either a P (pass) or an F (fail). In a regular graded course, an E earns no credit and 0 grade points, and it still counts in your GPA. A D isn't always enough. A D earns credit at KCTCS, but some courses require a C or better to pass or to count toward your program. FYE 100 is one of them: you need at least a C to pass. Check each syllabus, and ask your Success Coach which courses in your program have a C-or-better rule. Good to know You may see other grades on your record. A W (withdrawal), I (incomplete), or P (pass in a pass-fail course) doesn't count in your GPA. See the KCTCS catalog for the full list. 2 Weigh each grade by its credit hours Each course counts toward your GPA based on its credit hours. A 4-credit course has more impact than a 1-credit course, even if you earn the same grade in both. Multiply each course's grade points by its credit hours to get its quality points. Then divide the total quality points by the total credit hours. Course Credits Grade Grade points Quality points ENG 101 3 A 4.0 12.0 MAT 150 3 B 3.0 9.0 BIO 112 4 C 2.0 8.0 FYE 100 1 A 4.0 4.0 Totals 11 33.0 GPA = 33 ÷ 11 = 3.0 Pathfinder Tip Credit hours matter as much as grades. A C in a 4-credit course pulls your GPA down more than a C in a 1-credit course. When you're deciding where to put your study time, heavier courses deserve more of it. Look back at Lesson 5.1: Quantitative Reasoning . This is that skill, applied to your grades.

t: Wait... How Is My Grade Actually Calculated?
x: Try it Work each problem on your own first, on paper or in your head. Then open the answer to check yourself. Problem 1: Points-based You've earned 76 out of 100 possible points in a course so far. What's your grade percentage, and what letter grade is that? Show the answer 76 ÷ 100 = 76%, a C on a standard scale. Check your syllabus, since grade cutoffs can vary by course. Problem 2: GPA You take HIS 101 (3 credits) and earn a B, PSY 110 (3 credits) and earn an A, and MAT 110 (4 credits) and earn a C. What's your GPA? Show the answer Quality points: 3 × 3.0 = 9, 3 × 4.0 = 12, 4 × 2.0 = 8. Total 29 quality points ÷ 10 credits = 2.9 . Problem 3: Weighted A course weights exams at 60% and assignments at 40%. You score 70% on exams and 95% on assignments. What's your final grade? Show the answer 0.60 × 70 = 42, and 0.40 × 95 = 38. 42 + 38 = 80%, a B . Notice how the exam score held the grade down, even with strong assignments. Problem 4: What if? You have a 2.5 GPA after 20 credit hours. Next semester you take 12 credits and earn straight A's. Why does a higher-credit semester have more impact on your GPA than a lighter one? Show the answer Your old quality points are 2.5 × 20 = 50. The new semester adds 4.0 × 12 = 48. Your new GPA is 98 ÷ 32, about 3.06 . More credit hours means more quality points going into the average, so a heavier semester moves your GPA further, up or down.
Pull it together before you head back to your course. You've reached the end of Module 6. These are the ideas to carry forward.

Not a title. How you show up, especially when things change. 5 10 Essential Skills · #5 Adaptability & Leadership

What this skill is Leadership has less to do with a title than with how you show up, especially when things change. Adaptability & Leadership sounds like it belongs to people with corner offices and formal authority, but at the level this course focuses on, it's something much more immediate: contributing to a shared goal, adjusting when circumstances shift, and helping others stay on track when things get hard. You probably already do versions of all three. This module helps you see where and how. Leadership is a pattern of behavior more than a position, and you've been practicing it longer than you think.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You can describe how people cooperate to reach a common goal. You can explain how new situations may require doing things differently. You recognize how people motivate others to reach a goal. Milestone Your target You contribute toward reaching a common goal. You adjust to new situations by doing things differently and keeping a positive mindset. You encourage others to keep going toward their goals as situations change. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from understanding how these things work to actually doing them, in real situations, with real people, under real pressure.

What leadership actually looks like Most students hear "leadership" and think of student government, team captains, or supervisors. The Milestone level doesn't require any of that. What it asks for is showing up: contributing, adjusting, and encouraging, in whatever setting you're already in. What people assume it means Being in charge of a group Having a title or formal role Being the loudest or most confident person Making all the decisions Never struggling or needing help What it actually looks like Showing up consistently and following through Adjusting your approach when something isn't working Helping a teammate who's stuck, without being asked Staying steady when a plan falls apart Contributing your strengths to something shared

s: Where it shows up in this module
x: Where it shows up in this module This module's self-assessment work connects directly to Adaptability & Leadership, which is why it's the featured skill here. Strengths: how you adapt Your strengths say a lot about how you naturally respond to change and challenge. A student who leads through relationships adapts differently than one who leads through analysis. Neither is wrong, but knowing which one you are helps you use it on purpose instead of stumbling into it. Values: why you lead Your values are the reason you show up for things, the "why" behind your choices and commitments. When circumstances change and motivation gets harder, values are what anchor you. They're also what makes your leadership real rather than a performance. Blind spots: where to watch Every strength has an overuse pattern, and an overused strength can get in the way of adapting. The student who leads through decisiveness may struggle to adjust when the first plan fails. Naming your blind spot is the first step to managing it when things get hard. Self-knowledge: better leadership It's hard to lead others well if you don't understand yourself. The HIGH5 assessment and the Values Card Sort are leadership groundwork as well as personal reflection, and what you learn about yourself applies directly to how you show up for others.

In your own life Reflect Think of a time, this semester or before college, when something changed unexpectedly and you had to find a different approach. What did you do? What does that tell you about how you adapt? Is there someone in your life, at work, at home, or in a group, whom you quietly help stay on track or keep going? That's leadership. What strengths make you that person for them? When things get hard, what do you fall back on? A value, a habit, a person? Watch for where that anchor shows up in your results in this module.

How it shows up later Adaptability & Leadership is one of the strongest choices for your third STAR(T) Story, the one you pick. If you choose it, you'll write or record one story about a specific time you adapted, contributed, or helped others keep going through change. The self-knowledge you build in this module is the foundation of that story. It doesn't have to be dramatic. A moment when you kept going when you wanted to quit, and your persistence helped someone else keep going too, is a Milestone-level story. Start small and honest, and start noticing those moments now. The STAR(T) Stories Guide at the back of this book walks you through the whole capstone, with a practice guide for each story. Skill definition and Milestone indicators are based on the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education's Kentucky Graduate Profile .

Interests tell you what you enjoy. Values tell you who you are. We make decisions every day, some big, some small. But most of us rarely stop to ask why we choose what we choose. Behind every real decision sits something deeper than preference or convenience: your personal values. Values are the principles and beliefs that guide how you live, often without your noticing. They shape what you prioritize, what you say yes or no to, how you react under pressure, and the people and places you're drawn to. When your actions line up with your values, life tends to feel more meaningful and less stressful. When they don't, something feels off, even if you can't name exactly why. Interests tell you what you enjoy. Values tell you who you are.

What values actually shape Your values are working in the background of almost every important choice you make. They show up most clearly in these places. Your priorities What you actually spend time and energy on. Not what you say matters, but what you act like matters. Your boundaries What you'll say no to, even when it's inconvenient or disappoints someone. Your goals What you're working toward, and whether those goals feel like yours or borrowed from someone else. Your reactions Why some situations energize you and others drain you. Often it comes down to whether your values are being honored. Your relationships Who you're drawn to and who you clash with. Shared or clashing values explain a lot of both. Your career fit Whether a job or field feels sustainable over time, which often has as much to do with values as with interest.

s: Interests and values aren't the same thing
x: Interests and values aren't the same thing Many career tools, like the interest assessment you took in Module 6, focus on interests: what you enjoy, what you're curious about, what keeps you engaged. Interests matter, but they're only part of the picture. Look back at Lesson 6.2: The six interest types Interests What you enjoy or find engaging right now Can shift as you try new things and meet new people Often shaped by what you've been exposed to so far May not carry you when the work gets hard Useful for exploring directions Values What matters to you at a deeper level Tend to stay steadier across time and situations Often show up under pressure, when choices get hard Give meaning even when the work isn't exciting A more reliable compass for long-term decisions What the research says Research on values at work finds that when people's work fits their personal values, they tend to be more satisfied and more committed to it. Researchers also find that interests and values are related but measure different things. You can be very interested in something that clashes with your values, or committed to work that isn't exciting but feels deeply meaningful. Sources: Schwartz (1992); Sagiv & Schwartz (1995); Dobson et al. (2014); Arieli, Sagiv, & Roccas (2020).

If your interests keep shifting Some people move easily between interests, drawn to many subjects, fields, and activities over time. If that's you, following your interests from one thing to the next can feel exciting but directionless. Each interest feels real in the moment, but "What do I actually want to do?" stays unanswered. For people like this, values are often the more useful compass. They connect the dots between pursuits that look unrelated. Someone who values creativity, connection, and impact might find those values showing up in education, health care, design, or community work: very different fields, with the same underlying why. If your interests feel too varied to point anywhere, ask yourself: what do the things I keep coming back to have in common? The answer is usually a value, not an interest. Values can shift too, and that's normal Values tend to be steadier than interests, but they aren't fixed forever. What mattered most to you at 16 may look different at 20, 30, or 40. Big life experiences can clarify or shift what you prioritize. That's growth, not inconsistency. Looking at your values now gives you a clearer picture of who is actually showing up to college today, rather than who you were or who you think you should be.

The Values Card Sort The Values Card Sort helps you find your Top 5 core values, not by answering questions about yourself, but by choosing between values that all feel important. The sorting and narrowing is where the real reflection happens. Sort the cards Place each of 30 value cards into one of three piles: most important to you, somewhat important, and least important. Go with your gut. Narrow to five Keep narrowing until you have the five values that matter most to you right now. This is the hard part, and it's supposed to be. Save your results Save your Top 5 as a PDF or write them down before you close the page. You'll use them in the My Values Snapshot and in this module's journal or class discussion. Pathfinder Tip When two values feel equally important and you have to pick one, the one you keep coming back to is usually the more central value. Trust the pull, not the logic. Do the Values Card Sort Free, no account needed, and the site doesn't store your choices. Your instructor may also do a card sort in class. Go to the Values Card Sort

How to use your results Notice what's there Read each of your Top 5 and sit with it. Does it feel accurate? Does it surprise you? The values that were hardest to choose, or felt uncomfortable to claim, are often the most revealing. Look for the pattern Do your five cluster around a theme, like connection, achievement, freedom, or service? The pattern often says more than any single value about what drives you. Notice the gaps Is there a part of your life, like school, work, or relationships, where your values aren't being honored? That gap is often the source of a low-level dissatisfaction that's hard to name. Connect to decisions Think about a recent choice: a program, a job, a relationship. Does it line up with your values? If it does, it probably feels right even when it's hard. If it doesn't, that friction has a name now. Try it: My Values Snapshot Record your Top 5, why each one made the cut, one place your actions match your values, and one place there's a gap. Save it as a PDF and use it for this module's journal or class discussion. Open My Values Snapshot Knowing your values won't mean you have everything figured out, but it gives you a more honest picture of what matters to you right now, in this season of your life. That picture helps with the decisions ahead: which direction to explore, what kind of work might fit, and what you want college to be about. Your values will come up again in Mile Marker #7, in your career exploration in Module 8, and in your STAR(T) Stories.

t: What Are Strengths, and Why Do They Matter?
x: Not just what you're good at. What feels like you at your best. Most of us were taught to focus on what we're not good at: fix the weaknesses, fill the gaps, bring everything up to average. Strengths-based thinking flips that. Instead of asking "What's wrong with me?" it asks "What's already working, and how do I use more of it?" Strengths are the patterns of thinking, behaving, and interacting that come naturally to you. They feel energizing rather than draining, and they show up again and again in different situations. They're expressions of who you are, not only skills you've built. Strengths work is about using what already works, not fixing what doesn't.

t: What Are Strengths, and Why Do They Matter?
s: What strengths look like in real life
x: What strengths look like in real life Strengths aren't always obvious, especially to the person who has them. What feels easy to you often looks remarkable to someone else. Day to day, strengths can look like this: Staying calm when things go wrong Coming up with ideas quickly Helping others understand hard things Turning chaos into a workable plan Motivating people who are stuck Noticing details others miss Building trust quickly with strangers Asking questions that open things up Following through when others give up Everyone has strengths, even if you haven't named them yet. t: What Are Strengths, and Why Do They Matter?
x: What your results actually mean Your Top 5 strengths describe patterns, not boxes, and they don't lock you into a personality type. Think of them as a starting point for understanding how you naturally operate. They're most useful in four places. Look back at Lesson 7.1: Where Adaptability & Leadership shows up Learning Knowing your strengths helps you choose study strategies that work with how you think, not against it. A Thinker needs processing time before a discussion. A Deliverer thrives with clear checklists and deadlines. An Empathizer often learns best alongside other people. Working with others Your strengths shape how you collaborate, communicate, and show up in groups. A Coach is often the natural encourager in group work. A Catalyst pushes projects forward, sometimes faster than others can follow. A Thinker brings insight but may pull back when overwhelmed. Career direction Strengths give you clues about the settings and roles where you'll feel most alive, not just competent. You don't need to choose a major today. Notice what already fits. Empathizers are often drawn to helping professions, health care, advising, and education. Analysts to data, research, and problem-solving. Catalysts to leading and coordinating. Adapting to change This module's skill, Adaptability & Leadership, is closely tied to strengths. Knowing how you naturally respond to change lets you use that on purpose instead of just reacting. Under pressure, a Deliverer tends to get to work. An Optimist tends to reframe. Neither is wrong, but knowing which you are changes how you lead yourself and others.

t: What Are Strengths, and Why Do They Matter?
s: Every strength has a blind spot
x: Every strength has a blind spot Strengths are real and valuable, and every one of them has an overuse pattern. That's the nature of any real tendency: taken too far, or used in the wrong setting, even your best qualities can work against you. Key Term Blind spot: the overuse side of a strength, which is easy for you to miss and often easy for others to see. Deliverer May take on too much and burn out, or frustrate others by moving faster than they're ready. Analyst May overthink decisions or get stuck researching when it's time to act. Empathizer May struggle with boundaries or take on other people's stress. Catalyst May move faster than others can follow, or start things without finishing them. Thinker May pull back when overwhelmed, or get lost in ideas and miss the deadline. Optimist May avoid hard conversations or underestimate real risks. A blind spot is the shadow side of a real strength. Knowing yours lets you manage it instead of letting it manage you. The most useful move is simple: decide ahead of time what you'll do when you notice it showing up. Pathfinder Tip The blind spot question in Mile Marker #7 asks you to be honest, not hard on yourself. "I know I do this, and here's what it looks like" is a strength in itself.

t: What Are Strengths, and Why Do They Matter?
s: Using AI to understand your results
x: Using AI to understand your results AI Literacy BE Reflective AI can explain what a strength usually means and suggest ways to use it. What it can't do is tell you whether that description actually fits you. Only you can check it against your real life. Plain language: "Explain the HIGH5 strength Strategist in simple, everyday words." Putting it to work: "What are three study habits that fit someone whose top strengths include Deliverer and Empathizer?" Blind spots: "What does it look like when someone overuses the Catalyst strength, and what can they do about it?" You can share your strength names. Leave out your name and other personal details. Then ask yourself: does this sound like me? Where does it miss?
