Showing up in the conversation as someone worth listening to. 1 10 Essential Skills · #1 Communication

What this skill is Communication means more than talking or writing. It means showing up in the conversation as someone worth listening to. Communication shows up everywhere, but most people don't think about it until something goes wrong. A missed appointment because you didn't follow up. An instructor who didn't know you were struggling until it was too late. An advising session that felt generic because you didn't come with real questions. The conversations in this module, with your Success Coach, your instructors, and people in careers you're curious about, call for Milestone-level Communication: showing up as an active participant, not waiting to be told what to do. Benchmark communication gets you by. Milestone communication gets you what you need.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You ask questions to clarify your understanding. You express thoughts and ideas in writing. You share information in one-on-one and small-group conversations. Milestone Your target You give focused attention, ask clarifying questions, and notice nonverbal signals. You write formally and informally with logical structure, complete sentences, standard grammar, and correct punctuation. You take part in formal conversations with peers and professionals by offering information and ideas. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from reacting to engaging: from answering when asked to showing up with something to contribute.

s: The three Milestone behaviors, up close
x: The three Milestone behaviors, up close 1 Listen with focus, and ask clarifying questions Listening at the Milestone level is active. It means giving your full attention, not half-listening while you wait for your turn, noticing what's communicated beyond the words, and asking questions that show you processed what you heard. A basic question checks a box: "When is the deadline?" A clarifying question shows real engagement: "I want to make sure I understand. Does the prerequisite need to be done before I apply to the program, or just before I start it?" In an advising appointment, instead of nodding and hoping you understood, ask: "So just to confirm, if I take this course in the spring, I'm still on track to start the program in the fall?" 2 Write with structure and care Professional writing should be clear, organized, and respectful of the reader's time, without being stiff. At the Milestone level, you adjust to the situation: a text to a classmate looks different from an email to an instructor, which looks different from a message to an employer. Where this breaks down most often for college students is email. A one-line message with no greeting, no context, and no clear ask puts the work on the reader. An email that introduces you, explains your situation, and asks a clear question gets a faster, more useful reply. "hey when is the test" is Benchmark. The email example below is Milestone. 3 Come to professional conversations with something to offer This is the behavior most students underestimate. You don't need a script. You need to show up as a participant rather than a recipient: you bring your research, your questions, your thinking, and your goals. A student who says "I don't know what I want to take" is at Benchmark. A student who arrives with a draft schedule, two specific questions about course order, and a sense of their program direction is at Milestone, and gets a completely different kind of appointment. The same goes for career conversations and any time you talk with someone in a professional role. Come with something. Leave with something.

s: Where it shows up in this module
x: Where it shows up in this module This module puts you in the situations where the gap between Benchmark and Milestone is easiest to see. Your advising appointment Benchmark: You show up and wait to be told what to take. Milestone: You bring your Academic Planner , your Career Coach results, and specific questions about course order, prerequisites, or program requirements. You offer your thinking and refine it with your coach. A check-in with an instructor Benchmark: You avoid the conversation and hope things improve. Milestone: You send a clear, professional email that names the concern, says what you've tried, and asks a clear question. You make it easy for your instructor to help. Career conversations Benchmark: You ask "What do you do?" and listen. Milestone: You ask questions based on your research: about the day-to-day reality, the career path, what surprised them about the field. You share your own thinking and leave with something concrete. Group work Benchmark: You wait to be given a role and do your part. Milestone: You offer your strengths, notice when someone is struggling, ask clarifying questions about the task, and speak up when something isn't working, before it becomes a problem.

s: What a Milestone email looks like
x: What a Milestone email looks like Email is one of the most common ways you'll communicate professionally in college. Below is a Milestone-level email for a real situation. Example: a check-in email to an instructor To: Professor [Last Name] Subject: Question about my progress in [Course Name] Good afternoon, Professor [Last Name], My name is [First Name], and I'm in your [Course Name] class, section [number]. I'm writing because I'm concerned about my scores on the last two assignments and want to make sure I'm on track to finish the course well. I've reviewed your feedback, and I think I'm struggling most with [specific area]. I tried [something specific you did], which helped a little, but I'm still not confident I understand [specific concept]. Would you have time for a short meeting or office hours this week? I want to understand what to do differently before the next assignment. Thank you for your time. [First and Last Name] [Course and section] What makes it Milestone: it introduces the student, states the situation specifically, names what they've already tried, asks a clear question, and sounds professional without being stiff. It makes it easy for the instructor to say yes. Pathfinder Tip Before you send any professional email, read it once as the person receiving it. Does it give them enough context to help? Is the ask clear? Would you want to answer it? If not, revise before you send.

In your own life Reflect Think of a conversation that went better because you came prepared. What did you bring to it? Is there an email or conversation you've been putting off? What would a clear, specific version of it sound like? When someone explains something important to you, what helps you really listen, and what pulls your attention away?

How it shows up later Communication is the skill underneath every other skill in this course. You need it to speak up for yourself in advising, to ask for help before it's too late, to present yourself to employers, and to tell your STAR(T) Stories in a way that's clear, specific, and worth listening to. Every conversation, email, and appointment in this module is practice, so you're doing Communication, not only learning about it. Skill definition and Milestone indicators are based on the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education's Kentucky Graduate Profile .

What fits, what doesn't, and how to find out. A good career fit takes more than choosing something that "sounds cool" or "pays well." It means finding work that lines up with who you are: your values, strengths, interests, and how you actually want to live. In this lesson you'll use Career Coach and O*NET to explore options, then choose one career to research in depth with the Career Research Guide .

What career fit actually means Career fit happens when several parts of your life line up with what a career actually asks of you. You've already gathered most of this in earlier modules, and now you'll put it to work. Key Term Career fit: how well a career's real demands match who you are and how you want to live. Interests What you naturally enjoy doing or learning about. Module 6: your interest results Strengths What comes naturally: the patterns that energize you rather than drain you. Module 7: your HIGH5 strengths Values What matters most to you in work: stability, creativity, impact, independence, balance. Module 7: your Values Snapshot Work environment Fast or steady? Hands-on or thinking-based? Independent or on a team? Remote or in person? Research Guide, Section 3 Life management Schedule, pace, physical demands, how much time with people. Does the daily reality fit how you manage your time and energy? Module 3: your time and energy Education fit What credential are you willing and able to pursue, and does the path match your academic direction? Module 6: your Academic Planner Myth-buster You don't need to pick a career today. Many students start college without a set career, and plenty of people who do have one change direction along the way. This module is about exploring possibilities, not locking in a lifetime decision. Think less "What job am I going to do forever?" and more "What direction do I want to explore next?"

s: Think in directions, not job titles
x: Think in directions, not job titles Instead of hunting for the one perfect job, start with a career cluster: a group of related roles that share similar settings, skills, and values. A cluster gives you options and room to change course. Health care Business and finance IT and technology Human services Skilled trades Education Arts and design Public safety Engineering and STEM Manufacturing You don't need to choose the job yet, just a direction worth exploring. Pausing on purpose before you react, decide, or assume. 2 10 Essential Skills · #2 Critical & Creative Thinking

What this skill is Critical thinking means pausing on purpose before you react, decide, or assume. It has nothing to do with overthinking or arguing. You make dozens of decisions every day, some small, some major. Much of the stress that comes with them is really confusion: not being sure what's actually going on, what matters most, or what's even true. This module gives you a simple way to slow down, just for a moment, and think more clearly. That habit helps with more than schoolwork. It's the same thinking that builds an honest, specific STAR(T) story, and it's exactly the kind of thinking employers look for. Benchmark thinking reacts. Milestone thinking pauses, checks, and decides.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You describe a problem in general terms, based on whatever information you happen to have. You acknowledge your own perspective, but don't always notice how it's shaping your thinking. You come up with possible solutions, even if they're only loosely connected to the real problem. Milestone Your target You figure out what's really going on by finding and using relevant information, not just what's easiest to find. You seek out and consider other perspectives, not just your own first reaction. You name the patterns, relationships, and context that matter, and use them to reach a clear, informed conclusion. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from reacting to checking: from going with your first read of a situation to actually examining it before you decide.

s: The three Milestone behaviors, up close
x: The three Milestone behaviors, up close 1 Figure out what's really going on At the Milestone level, you don't react to the first version of a problem you see. You pause long enough to ask, "What's actually happening here, and what do I need to know before I respond?" This is the difference between assuming and checking. An assumption is something you treat as true without checking it. Milestone thinking notices the assumption and asks whether it's actually true, or just the first thing that came to mind. Instead of "This assignment makes no sense," ask: "What is the professor actually asking me to do, and where can I check?" 2 Look for other perspectives Your first take on a situation is shaped by your experiences, your mood, and your assumptions, and it isn't always the full picture. Milestone thinking means considering how someone else might see the same situation, especially before you decide something is "obviously" true. The goal is to catch the moments when your read might be incomplete and ask what you might be missing, not to doubt yourself constantly. Instead of assuming a coworker is ignoring you, ask: "Could they be busy or distracted? What else could explain this?" 3 Name what matters, and why This is where critical thinking becomes a tool you can use. It means being able to name the real question, what matters most in the situation, which information is solid and which is shaky, and what's likely to happen depending on what you choose. That's exactly what the 4C Check walks you through, and it's the same thinking that turns a vague STAR(T) story into one that's specific, honest, and worth telling. "If I drop this class, what does that actually mean for my financial aid, my schedule next semester, and when I finish?" That's thinking through consequences, not guessing.

Where it shows up Everyday decisions Benchmark: You go with your gut and move on. Milestone: You notice the thinking trap, ask what's actually true, and consider what matters most before deciding. News and social media Benchmark: If it sounds right, you accept it. Milestone: You ask: Is this source credible? Is this fact, an ad, or someone's opinion? Your STAR(T) story Benchmark: You pick an experience because it sounds impressive and write something generic. Milestone: You use the 4C Check to make sure your story is clear, accurate, and shows what you want it to show. Using AI tools Benchmark: Whatever AI gives you feels like an answer. Milestone: You pause, check it against what you know, and decide whether it's useful before you use it.

In your own life Reflect Think of a time you reacted fast and later wished you'd paused. What would one good question have changed? Who in your life sees situations very differently than you do? What could you learn from how they'd read a problem? What's one decision in front of you right now that deserves a slower, more careful look?

How it shows up later Critical thinking is a habit you build with practice, not a personality trait. You don't have to feel like "a critical thinker" for this to work. You only have to practice the pause: stop, ask one good question, then decide. It's one of the most consistently valued skills in any job, any relationship, and any decision you'll face. It's also a strong choice for the third skill in your STAR(T) Stories . Skill definition and Milestone indicators are based on the Kentucky Council on Postsecondary Education's Kentucky Graduate Profile .

It's not overthinking. It's thinking with intention. Critical thinking doesn't require being "smart," complicated, or argumentative. It's the simple skill of pausing long enough to ask better questions before you react, decide, or assume something is true. It helps you make better decisions, avoid costly mistakes, stay calm instead of jumping to conclusions, understand instructions, evaluate information (especially online), solve problems with more confidence, and communicate more clearly. Critical thinking is thinking on purpose.

What it is, and isn't Critical thinking means you Slow down long enough to consider what's really going on Ask questions instead of assuming Look for evidence instead of guessing Make choices based on clarity, not impulse or pressure Critical thinking is not Overthinking Being negative Criticizing others Arguing for the sake of arguing Trying to "sound smart" Doing everything alone It's intentional, not automatic: simply pausing to think clearly before you act.

Four habits of strong thinkers These habits are small, but they're powerful. You don't need all of them all the time. Noticing even one in the moment can change how a situation plays out. 1. Curiosity They ask, "What do I need to know?" or "What am I missing?" 2. Clarity They make sure they understand the instructions, situation, or problem before moving forward. 3. Checking They double-check sources, facts, and assumptions instead of taking the first answer at face value. 4. Calm decisions They don't rush. They think it through, even when there's pressure to decide fast.

s: What it looks like in real life
x: What it looks like in real life Critical thinking shows up everywhere, not only in school. These examples show what happens when someone pauses long enough to ask a better question. At school Instead of "This assignment makes no sense," you ask: "What is the professor actually asking me to do?" At work Instead of assuming a coworker is ignoring you, you ask: "Could they just be busy or distracted?" In your personal life Instead of reacting right away to a text, you pause and ask: "What's the most helpful way to respond?" In big decisions Instead of choosing a major because "everyone else is," you ask: "How does this fit my strengths, values, and goals?" You don't have to feel like "a critical thinker" for this to work. It's a habit, not a personality trait, and habits get stronger with practice. The next lesson, Spotting Assumptions, Biases & Thought Traps , looks at what gets in the way of clear thinking. Look back at Lesson 7.2 : your values are a big part of "what matters to me."

Everyone falls into these patterns. The trick is noticing them. You can't think clearly if you don't notice what's messing with your thinking. Critical thinking also means noticing the invisible forces that shape your thinking without your realizing it. Everyone falls into these patterns sometimes, and doing so doesn't make you a bad thinker. This lesson covers three of the biggest obstacles to clear thinking: assumptions , biases , and thought traps . Once you can recognize them, you can make better decisions, communicate more clearly, and avoid a lot of unnecessary stress.

Assumptions: the invisible fill-in-the-blank Assumptions are things we treat as true without checking. They usually fill the gap when we don't have enough information. "The professor probably hates me." "There's no way I can afford college." "My advisor won't have time to help." "My friend is ignoring me on purpose." Clear thinking starts with one question: "Is that actually true, or is it something I'm assuming?" Key Term Assumption: something you treat as true without checking it.

s: Biases: the lens that colors your thinking
x: Biases: the lens that colors your thinking A bias is a natural tendency to see things a certain way, usually shaped by your past experiences or preferences. Biases are mental shortcuts, and shortcuts aren't always bad, but in decisions they can lead you off track. Four common ones: Key Term Bias: a built-in tendency to see things a certain way, often without noticing. Confirmation bias Looking for information that supports what you already believe, and ignoring what doesn't. "I already think this class is going to be awful, so everything confirms it." Familiarity bias Choosing what feels familiar, even when it isn't the best choice. "I'll pick the same major my friends are in." Halo effect Letting one positive trait shape your whole opinion of someone or something. "They're confident, so they must be right." Negativity bias Paying more attention to negative experiences or feedback than to positive ones. "I messed up once, so I must be bad at this."

s: Thought traps: the quicksand of clear thinking
x: Thought traps: the quicksand of clear thinking Thought traps are automatic, unhelpful shortcuts we all fall into. They feel true in the moment, but they're rarely accurate. Jumping to conclusions Deciding something with little or no evidence. "My instructor hasn't answered yet. They must be mad." All-or-nothing thinking Seeing things as only good or bad, success or failure. "If I mess up this exam, my future is over." Overgeneralizing Letting one experience define everything. "I struggled with math once, so I'll always struggle." Mind reading Deciding you know what someone else is thinking. "They didn't smile at me. They must not like me." Catastrophizing Expecting the worst case by default. "If I change my major, I'll ruin my whole life."

Why this matters Assumptions, biases, and thought traps can quietly affect: Assignment choices Test anxiety Academic planning Career decisions Relationships and group work Talking with instructors Your confidence Noticing them gives you back control.

Quick practice: spot the trap For each statement, name what's going wrong. Then open the answer to check yourself. "I didn't understand the first chapter, so I know I'll fail the class." Show the answer Overgeneralizing and catastrophizing: one hard chapter becomes a failed class. "My advisor hasn't emailed me back yet. They probably don't care." Show the answer Jumping to conclusions, with a little mind reading. A slow reply has plenty of other explanations. "Everyone else seems to know what they're doing. I'm the only one struggling." Show the answer An assumption, plus overgeneralizing. You can't see how other people are really doing, and almost every student feels this way at some point. Pathfinder Tip You won't get rid of these patterns completely, and you don't need to. The goal is to notice them in the moment, often enough that they stop running the show. Next, the 4C Check gives you a simple tool to use instead.

t: The 4C Check: A Simple Tool for Better Decisions
x: Pause, get clear, and choose wisely. Most of the stress in a hard decision comes from confusion, not from the decision itself. "What should I major in?" "Should I drop this class?" "Should I take that job?" "Should I bring this up or let it go?" Critical thinking gets easier when you have a simple tool to walk through a decision step by step, and the 4C Check is that tool.

t: The 4C Check: A Simple Tool for Better Decisions
x: The four Cs C1 Clarity: What am I really deciding? A lot of poor decisions come from being unclear about the actual question. Strong feelings and quick assumptions can blur it, so name them and set them aside for a moment. "Do I hate this class, or am I just overwhelmed this week?" "Am I unsure about the major, or just nervous about one course?" "Is the relationship the problem, or the way we communicate?" Ask: What is the exact decision I'm trying to make? C2 Context: What matters most here? Name your priorities, values, and limits, and consider how the situation looks from someone else's point of view. "My priority is finishing on time." "I need flexibility because of childcare." "I value honesty, even when it's awkward." "How would my instructor see this?" Ask: What factors matter most for me right now, and whose view am I missing? C3 Credibility: What do I know, and what am I assuming? Check the quality of your information. Separate what you know from what you're assuming or have only heard. Solid: your advisor, the catalog, the syllabus, official information. "MAT 150 is required for my program." Shaky: rumors, guesses, assumptions. "Someone said this instructor is impossible." "AI told me this is the transfer requirement. Did I check it against the actual catalog?" Ask: What do I know for sure, and what do I need to check? C4 Consequences: What might happen next? Name your realistic options and think one step ahead for each, not ten. Then choose the most reasonable next step. "If I drop this class, will it delay when I finish?" "If I send this message, will it help or make things worse?" "If I take this job, how will it affect my schedule?" "If I let AI write my whole email to my instructor, how will I sound, and how will I answer if they write back with a question?" Ask: What are my options, what's likely to happen with each, and what's my next step? Pathfinder Tip You won't always need all four. Sometimes naming the real question (Clarity) or checking your information (Credibility) is enough to see things differently. Save the full check for decisions that feel bigger or stickier than they should. Look back at Lesson 4.3: SIFT is Credibility for anything you read online.

t: Think It Through: Using Critical Thinking to Build Your STAR(T) Story
x: STAR(T) in five steps STAR(T) is the framework for your capstone: a short, true story about a time you showed a skill, told in five steps. S Situation: What was going on? Set the scene. T Task: What needed to happen, and what was your role? A Action: What did you specifically do? Not the group. You. R Result: What happened? What changed? T Transfer: Why does it matter going forward, for your next class, a future job, or your life? The focus is on "I" because the Action step is where the skill lives. If you describe what the group did, no one can see what you did. Transfer matters because it's where you show you learned something and know where you're taking it. Go deeper The STAR(T) Stories Guide covers each step in detail, with a full example and practice guides for your capstone stories.

t: Think It Through: Using Critical Thinking to Build Your STAR(T) Story
s: Where thought traps sneak into STAR(T) drafts
x: Where thought traps sneak into STAR(T) drafts The thought traps from Lesson 9.3 show up in STAR(T) stories all the time. They just look a little different. "We" instead of "I" It's tempting to describe the Action as something the group did, especially if it feels safer or more humble. But STAR(T) is about your role. Before We decided to split up the project and get it done. After I noticed we were behind, so I suggested splitting the project and volunteered to take the research section. All-or-nothing results Results don't have to be dramatic to be real. All-or-nothing thinking pushes you to inflate a result or dismiss it, when the honest answer is somewhere in between. Before Everything worked out perfectly in the end. After We finished on time and got good feedback, though I'd plan the timeline differently next time. Picking a story because it sounds impressive This is the "sounding smart" trap from Lesson 9.2 . A story that sounds good but isn't quite true, or that you can't talk about in detail, won't hold up to a follow-up question. Instead Pick a story you remember well enough to talk about for two more minutes if someone asked. A vague Transfer Overgeneralizing shows up as a Transfer that could fit any story at all. Before This experience taught me a lot and will help me in college and my career. Instead Name the specific thing: what will you do differently, and in what kind of situation? AI Literacy BE Reflective If you use AI to help brainstorm your story, watch especially for the vague Transfer. AI-written Transfer statements often sound polished but generic. Make sure the final version sounds like you and says something specific to your experience. A note on choosing your story Don't avoid a story just because things didn't go the way you wanted. A story where something went wrong, and you can honestly name what you learned or would do differently, often shows clearer thinking than one where everything worked out. "I made the wrong call, here's how I noticed, and here's what I'd do differently" shows judgment, honesty, and growth, and for many people it's the stronger story.

t: Think It Through: Using Critical Thinking to Build Your STAR(T) Story
s: Run your draft through the 4C Check
x: Run your draft through the 4C Check Once you have a draft, the 4C Check is a fast way to find the soft spots: the places where your story could be clearer, more accurate, or more specific. Example: a student is drafting a story about asking an instructor for an extension after falling behind because of a work schedule change. C1 Clarity: What story am I actually telling? Before I had a lot going on and emailed my professor about an assignment. After My work hours changed with two days' notice, and the new schedule ran right into the deadline for a major paper. C2 Context: What mattered most here? The student realizes the real priority was keeping a good working relationship with the instructor while being honest about a real limit, not only getting an extension. C3 Credibility: Is this accurate, or did I round up? Before I handled it really well, and my professor was super impressed. After My professor gave me a two-day extension and said they appreciated the early heads-up. C4 Consequences: So what? What does this mean going forward? Before This taught me communication is important. After Now, when something unexpected comes up, I contact the person affected as soon as I know, not after I've already missed something. Pathfinder Tip Don't aim for a perfect story. Aim for a true one you understand well enough to talk about. The 4C Check is there to make sure your story is clear, accurate, and actually says something, not to make it sound better.

Yes, the group work skill. Stay with us. This one's worth it. 8 10 Essential Skills · #8 Collaboration & Teamwork

What this skill is Yes, the group work skill. Stay with us. This one's worth it. If you groaned a little when you saw this module's skill, you're not alone. Most people have at least one group project story that still makes them tense up: the partner who disappeared, the group member who took over everything, the project that fell apart two days before it was due. Most students don't know that instructors often groan too. Group work has a reputation problem on both sides of the classroom. So this module won't pretend group work is great. It will help you understand why it so often goes badly, starting with how you tend to operate, so you can do something about it next time. Benchmark collaboration shows up. Milestone collaboration makes the group better.

Where you're headed Below, in plain terms, is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You support team decisions by taking part in discussions. You respond promptly to messages and requests for information. You complete your tasks on time and see how your part affects the team. You recognize your own strengths and limits within a team. Milestone Your target You contribute ideas that fit the team's actual goals, not just any idea. You address conflict constructively, saying what you expect and adjusting your own behavior based on feedback. You figure out what tasks are needed and learn your teammates' strengths, so roles get divided fairly. You adapt to changing plans and roles in ways that build trust and respect. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from "doing your part" to paying attention to how the team is working, and doing something about it when it isn't.

s: The four Milestone behaviors, up close
x: The four Milestone behaviors, up close 1 Contribute ideas that fit the actual goal At the Benchmark level, "contributing" can mean almost anything: agreeing with whatever's already been decided, or tossing out an idea that's interesting but unrelated to what the team is trying to do. At the Milestone level, your contributions are tied to what the team is trying to accomplish. That means understanding the goal well enough to know whether an idea moves the team toward it, and being willing to say so, even if it means setting aside an idea you personally like. Instead of "We should also add a section about X" (because it interests you), ask: "Does X help us do what the assignment is asking for?" 2 Address conflict constructively This is probably the biggest gap between Benchmark and Milestone, and the source of most group work horror stories. At the Benchmark level, conflict tends to get avoided (hoping it fixes itself), absorbed (quietly doing extra work to make up for it), or escalated (going straight to the instructor without talking to the group first). At the Milestone level, conflict gets addressed directly: you say what you need or expect, and you're willing to adjust your own behavior based on feedback, not just wait for others to change. Instead of silently redoing a teammate's section because it "wasn't right," try: "I noticed we have different ideas about how this section should look. Can we talk about what we're each picturing?" 3 Know the tasks, and know your team A lot of group trouble starts before anyone does any work. Nobody spells out what the project needs, so roles land by accident: whoever speaks first, whoever cares most, or whoever feels guilty. At the Milestone level, you help the group name the tasks, then match them to people's strengths. That's what makes the work fair, and it's why understanding your own style (and asking about other people's) matters so much in this module. Instead of "I'll just do the slides because nobody else will," ask: "What does this project need, and who's strongest at what?" See also Lesson 10.5, Strategy 3: Play to your strengths Trail Tip: Divide & Conquer, AI-Style 4 Adapt to change without losing trust Group projects almost never go exactly as planned. Someone's role changes, a deadline moves, the assignment gets clarified halfway through. Benchmark collaboration treats these changes as disruptions. Milestone collaboration treats them as normal, and handles them in a way that keeps the group working well together. This is where trust gets built or lost. A team that can absorb a change without anyone feeling blindsided, dismissed, or stuck with extra work is a team that's actually collaborating, not just dividing up tasks. If a teammate has to step back because of a work or family emergency, Milestone collaboration means adjusting the plan together, not quietly resenting them or scrambling alone.

Where it shows up This module gives you a tool, your 16Personalities results, to understand your own collaboration tendencies before you're in the middle of a group situation. A group project forms Benchmark: You wait to see what role you get assigned. Milestone: You already know whether you tend to take charge, prefer to support, need structure, or work best with flexibility, and you say so early. Someone goes quiet Benchmark: You assume they don't care, and either pick up the slack silently or write them off. Milestone: You see a moment for direct, low-drama communication, and you reach out before it becomes a bigger problem. Two people disagree Benchmark: You stay quiet and hope it resolves on its own, or pick a side privately. Milestone: You treat the disagreement as information about priorities, working styles, or unclear expectations, not just a personality clash. The plan changes Benchmark: You feel thrown off and frustrated that the plan isn't the plan anymore. Milestone: You expect it, and focus on how to adjust together rather than who's to blame. Pathfinder Tip You don't have to become a different kind of person to be good at this. The goal is to know your own tendencies well enough to use them on purpose, not to turn introverts into extraverts or planners into improvisers, and to understand that other people's tendencies aren't wrong, just different.

In your own life Reflect Think of your best group experience, at school, at work, in your community, or on a team. What made it work? Think of one that went sideways. Which of the four behaviors was missing? When conflict shows up in a group, do you tend to avoid it, absorb it, or escalate it?

How it shows up later Collaboration isn't a "soft skill" in the sense of being optional or easy. In a recent national survey of employers, teamwork ranked second only to problem-solving among the skills they look for on a new graduate's resume. Almost nothing important gets built by one person alone. In this module, you'll build a real profile of how you work with others, strengths, struggles, and all, that you can use. It's also a strong choice for the third skill in your STAR(T) Stories . Employer data: National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE), Job Outlook 2025 . t: Who Are You in a Group?
x: Before you can work well with others, you have to understand how you naturally show up. Before you can work well with others, you have to understand how you naturally show up. College, work, and life all ask you to collaborate: sometimes with people you like, sometimes with people you've just met, and sometimes with people who work very differently than you do. Collaboration is more than "group work." It's communicating clearly, handling different personalities, sharing responsibilities, working through disagreements, following through, respecting differences, and contributing your strengths. This lesson starts with the most overlooked piece of all: your own default tendencies.

t: Who Are You in a Group?
s: How we tend to show up in groups
x: How we tend to show up in groups Most people have a "default mode" when working with others. You might recognize yourself in one of these, or in a mix of two or three. The Starter You jump in quickly, share ideas early, and get others moving. The Organizer You love timelines, steps, and lists, and making sure things get done. The Analyzer You ask questions, look at details, and make sure decisions make sense. The Doer You take action, handle tasks, and keep the project moving forward. The Encourager You support the group, check on everyone, and keep the mood positive. The Quiet Worker You prefer clear instructions, space to think, and tasks you can complete on your own. The Big-Picture Thinker You focus on goals, vision, where this is going, and creative solutions. None of these is better or worse. All of them matter, and a strong group usually has several working together. Pathfinder Tip If you thought, "I'm a mix of three of these, depending on the situation," that's normal, and it's useful information. Notice which one shows up most when you're stressed, and which one shows up when things are going smoothly.

t: Who Are You in a Group?
x: Where collaboration gets messy Problems usually start when people don't recognize, or don't communicate, their own tendencies. It can look like this: The Starter feels frustrated that no one else jumps in. The Quiet Worker feels steamrolled by louder voices. The Organizer gets stressed when others don't follow the plan. The Doer takes on too much and burns out. The Big-Picture Thinker gets bored with the details. The Analyzer slows things down when others want speed. These are style differences, not personal flaws. This module helps you figure out your own style, how to communicate it, and how to understand other people's, so these moments turn into conversations instead of resentment.

t: Who Are You in a Group?
x: Why personality tools can help Next, you'll take the 16Personalities assessment. Think of it as a tool for self-awareness and for understanding others, not a label. It can help you think about: How you prefer to communicate How you respond to stress How you take in information How you make decisions How you work in groups Knowing your tendencies makes collaboration less stressful and more realistic, for you and for everyone you work with.

t: Who Are You in a Group?
x: Start your snapshot Reflect Which group role feels most like you? What's one thing you know you do well when working with others? What's one thing that tends to frustrate you in group work, and why? Do you prefer leading, contributing, organizing, or supporting? Why? Take the 16Personalities assessment and make sense of your results. Understanding how you communicate, take in information, and work with others begins with understanding yourself. Everyone interacts, learns, and collaborates differently, and that's a strength, not a flaw. Knowing your tendencies can help you communicate more clearly, avoid misunderstandings, work better with people who think differently than you, and understand why certain group situations feel easy and others feel hard. In this lesson you'll take the free 16Personalities assessment and learn what your results mean. The point is self-awareness , the foundation of strong collaboration, not a label.

Take the assessment Go to 16personalities.com Start the free test. It takes about 10 minutes. The free results are all you need, so skip any paid upgrades. Answer honestly There are no right or wrong answers. Go with your first instinct, and answer for how you usually are, not how you think you should be. Get your type Your result is a four-letter type plus a fifth letter after a dash, like ENFP-T or ISTJ-A , along with a short description and a type name. Good to know 16Personalities uses the four-letter codes made famous by the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator, but it isn't the Myers-Briggs. It's its own model, built on the "Big Five" personality traits that psychology researchers use most.

Understand your letters Each letter comes from a pair. Together they give clues about how you operate in groups, communicate, make decisions, and handle stress. Most people land somewhere between the two ends of each pair, so read your percentages too, not just the letter. Energy How you recharge I · Introverted Energized by quiet time. Tends to think things through first. E · Extraverted Energized by people. Tends to talk things out. Mind How you take in information S · Observant Practical and down-to-earth. Likes concrete details and clear steps. N · Intuitive Imaginative and curious. Likes patterns, big ideas, and possibilities. Nature How you make decisions T · Thinking Leads with logic and fairness. F · Feeling Leads with values, harmony, and how people are affected. Tactics How you approach plans J · Judging Likes plans, organization, and predictability. P · Prospecting Likes flexibility, improvising, and keeping options open. Identity How you handle pressure -A · Assertive Tends to feel steady and self-assured under stress. -T · Turbulent Tends to feel stress more and push hard to improve. None of these is good or bad. They're different ways of being effective. A Turbulent result doesn't mean you're fragile, and an Assertive one doesn't mean you never worry.

s: How your type can show up in groups
x: How your type can show up in groups Your tendencies might shape: How you communicate. Extraverts often talk it out; introverts often think first, then speak. How you take on tasks. Observant types want the details; Intuitive types want the big picture first. How you make decisions. Thinking types aim for logic; Feeling types weigh how people will be affected. How you handle deadlines. Judging types want a plan early; Prospecting types need room to adjust. How conflict feels. Feeling types may avoid it; Thinking types may take it head-on. Your brain's wiring shapes collaboration too, whether or not you have a name for it. The next lesson looks at that, along with the strengths and struggles that come with each tendency. Look back at Lesson 7.3: Strengths . Your HIGH5 results and your type are two different lenses on the same person.

A map, not a rulebook Your personality type is not your identity, and it doesn't decide what you can or can't do. Personality tests describe tendencies, and your results can shift depending on your mood, your season of life, or how you read a question. Think of your type as a map of how you tend to operate, not a box you're stuck in. If part of your result doesn't sound like you, trust yourself. Noticing what doesn't fit is just as useful as noticing what does.

Your first impressions Reflect Which parts of your type feel accurate? What surprised you, or what do you disagree with? What described you well in group situations? What made you think, "Hmm, that explains a lot"? Record your type and first impressions in Step 2 of the Collaboration Snapshot . Just for fun Once you know your type, look it up on Frank James's YouTube channel . His short videos about each type are funny, and often uncomfortably accurate. Take them as entertainment, not science.

Every style has strengths and challenges. Knowing yours is power. Every collaboration style has strengths and challenges, and knowing yours gives you more control. Now that you've explored your 16Personalities results, it's time to connect them to how you work with others : what you bring to a team, what drains you, how you communicate, where misunderstandings happen, and what you need to do your best work. There are no good or bad personality types for collaboration, and the more you understand your tendencies, the easier it gets.

Your type and collaboration Each tendency tends to bring a strength to a group, and a struggle to watch for. Find your letters. Trait Strength Struggle to watch for Extraverted (E) Energizes the group, brings ideas forward May talk over quieter members Introverted (I) Thoughtful insight, calm presence May feel overshadowed or unheard Observant (S) Practical, detail-oriented, grounded May get frustrated by vague or "too theoretical" plans Intuitive (N) Creative solutions, big-picture thinking May skip steps or overlook details Thinking (T) Logic, clarity, fairness May come across as blunt or detached Feeling (F) Empathy, harmony, connection May avoid conflict, even when it's needed Judging (J) Organization, structure, follow-through May get stressed when plans change Prospecting (P) Flexible, adaptable, spontaneous May put things off or resist schedules These are tendencies, not weaknesses, and every team needs all kinds.

Different brains, different teammates Not everyone's brain works the same way, and that's normal. Some students identify as neurodivergent (ADHD, autism, dyslexia, anxiety-related processing differences, and more). Others simply notice they think or work differently from the people around them. You do not need a diagnosis to recognize a pattern. Look back at Divergent Minds: Your Brain, Your Way , the Module 3 bonus read, covers how these patterns show up in time and energy, too. Strengths different brains may bring Deep focus on meaningful tasks Creativity and big-picture thinking Spotting patterns quickly Thinking outside the box Honesty, clarity, and directness Deep empathy or attention to detail Challenges that may come up Overwhelm in noisy or chaotic groups Difficulty switching tasks Trouble with timing, planning, or transitions Missing social cues, or tone in texts Frustration with vague expectations Anxiety that affects speaking up Shutdown or overload moments in group settings Knowing your patterns, whether they come from personality, experience, or how your brain is wired, helps you ask for what you need and choose strategies that work for you. Knowing that other people have patterns too helps you collaborate more respectfully and patiently. What you share about yourself, and with whom, is always your choice. You can name what helps ("I work best with written deadlines") without explaining why.

Name your strengths These are common collaboration strengths. Which ones fit you? You're probably strong in more than one. Choose strategies that match how you work. Once you understand how you work, you can choose strategies that help you work well with others. Strong teamwork doesn't require being outgoing, loud, organized, or perfect. It comes from knowing how you operate, what you need, and how to say so respectfully. Collaboration gets much easier when you use strategies that match your strengths and support your challenges. These nine work in classes, study groups, jobs, and everyday relationships, and you'll pick three of them for Mile Marker #10.

Nine strategies Start with clear expectations A lot of group conflict comes from unclear roles and unclear goals. Early on, get answers to four questions: What's the task? What are the deadlines? Who's doing what? What does "done" look like? This lowers stress for everyone, especially people who like structure. Communicate your style, respectfully Simple scripts work wonders: "I work best when tasks are clearly divided." "I can take the lead on organizing, but I need others to jump in with ideas." "I like to think for a moment before I respond." "Group chaos overwhelms me. Can we set a quick plan?" "I do better with deadlines written down." "I'm happy to help with research, but I don't love presenting." Saying it up front helps the group work smarter. It isn't making excuses. Play to your strengths Use what you naturally do well, from the group roles in Lesson 10.2 : Organizer: manage the timeline or checklist Analyzer: check accuracy and details Starter: open discussions or brainstorm Encourager: support morale and help settle conflict Doer: take on the task-heavy pieces Quiet Worker: tackle clear, independent tasks Big-Picture Thinker: propose creative solutions or direction Let strengths lead, and let others cover what drains you. Ask clarifying questions Clarifying questions prevent most miscommunication: "What do you mean by that?" "Can you give an example?" "What's the top priority here?" "What's our next step?" "Where should this information go?" Clarifying is smart teamwork. Break tasks into manageable pieces If the group is stuck, overwhelmed, or putting things off, try breaking the project into smaller tasks, giving each one a lead person, setting mini-deadlines, and meeting briefly to check in. It helps anyone who struggles to get started, and honestly, it helps everyone. Use your tools wisely Tools that structure the work make collaboration easier: a shared Word document in OneDrive, Microsoft Teams, a group text or GroupMe, a shared checklist or task board, or an outline template everyone fills in. Assume good intent, most of the time People usually aren't ignoring you; they're busy. They usually aren't trying to be rude; they're stressed. They usually aren't lazy; they're overwhelmed. Assuming good intent prevents a lot of unnecessary conflict. But "most of the time" matters. If you need clarity, ask. If something feels off, address it calmly. If you feel disrespected, set a boundary. Know your stress signals Everyone has a collaboration stress mode. Some common signals: Shutting down Over-controlling Withdrawing Doing everything yourself Procrastinating Avoiding meetings Getting rigid Your stress signals are information, not failures. Use them as a cue to pause and choose a strategy that helps. Use the 2-minute reset When tension rises: pause , breathe , then ask yourself three questions: "What's actually the issue?" "What matters most here?" "What's the next best step?" It gives your brain a chance to respond instead of react. Pathfinder Tip If the 2-minute reset sounds familiar, it should. It's the same move as the 4C Check from Module 9: pause, get clear, then decide. The thinking tools in this course connect, and they show up everywhere, including in the middle of a group chat that's going sideways.

Use AI to turn a group assignment into tasks, roles, and a timeline. Using AI to turn "someone should probably..." into an actual plan. Almost everyone in a group project has lived through this scene. The group agrees the project needs a topic, research, slides, and a presentation. Everyone nods. Nobody assigns anything. A week goes by, and now it's due Friday and somehow it's everyone's problem at once. A lot of group tension has less to do with people being lazy or difficult than with one simple problem: nobody wants to be the one who assigns tasks to other people. It can feel bossy or awkward. So nothing gets assigned, and the group just hopes. AI is great at being the "bad guy" who hands out the to-do list, so no one in your group has to be. This Trail Tip shows you how to use AI to break an assignment into tasks, suggest roles, and build a realistic timeline, fast. Your group still makes the real decisions. AI gets you past the awkward "okay... so... who's doing what?" silence.

How to do it Check the AI rules first Look at the assignment's AI use label and the course AI policy. Planning with AI is usually fine even when the work itself has to be your own, but check. Paste in the assignment instructions The more AI knows about what's required, the more useful the plan will be. Add your group's roles and the due date Use "Member A, Member B" instead of names, or ask your group before you share their first names. Their information isn't yours to share. Ask for tasks, roles, a timeline, and group norms Use the prompt below. All four together turn a vague assignment into something your group can act on today. Bring the plan back to your group, and adjust it AI doesn't know who's great at design or who works on Tuesdays. Use the plan as a first draft, not a final ruling. Try this prompt "We're working on a group project for [class]. Here are the assignment instructions: [paste]. There are [number] of us, Member A through Member [letter], and the project is due [date]. Please build a simple group work plan with: 1) the main tasks, 2) suggested roles so everyone contributes, 3) a weekly timeline, 4) a few earlier check-in dates so we're not rushing at the end, and 5) four or five simple group norms for how we'll communicate and stay organized. Keep it simple, realistic, and student-friendly, with headings and bullet points."

What you'll get back This condensed sample plan is for a four-person psychology presentation: Sample AI-generated group plan (condensed) Main tasks Choose a topic · Research (3+ credible sources) · Build an outline · Build slides · Prepare and practice the presentation Suggested roles Member Role Focus A Project organizer Tracks deadlines, coordinates the group B Research lead Finds sources, shares notes C Slide designer Builds and organizes slides D Presentation lead Organizes speaking parts, leads practice Weekly timeline Week 1: choose topic, assign roles, find 2+ sources Week 2: finish research, build outline, start slides Week 3: finish slides, assign speaking parts, practice Group norms Respond to group messages within 24 hours Finish assigned tasks before meetings Speak up early if you're stuck or confused Respect each other's ideas and working styles Pathfinder Tip This is Strategy 1, Start with clear expectations , on fast-forward. AI gives your group a first draft to react to, instead of a blank page to build from. Then use what you know about each other's strengths to adjust the roles.

Starting with the parts of "society" you're already standing in. 7 10 Essential Skills · #7 Civic Engagement

What this skill is Engaging in civic life to improve society, starting with the parts of "society" you're already standing in. "Civic engagement" tends to bring certain images to mind: voting, city council meetings, protests, campaigns. Those are real examples. They can also feel intimidating if you're not there yet, and they can make this skill seem like something for other people , people older, more political, or more "into that kind of thing" than you. Every one of those bigger examples is built on a smaller foundation: the everyday ability to engage with the people and systems around you, notice how things actually work, and help make a shared space better. You don't have to wait to build that. You're building it right now, in the communities you're already part of. Benchmark civic engagement notices the conversation. Milestone civic engagement joins it, and helps move it somewhere.

Where you're headed Below is the difference between where most students start and where you're headed. This skill's official language talks about public policy and government, because that's where it's ultimately pointing. You'll build toward it in smaller spaces first. See also Lesson 1.2 explains Benchmark, Milestone, and Capstone. Benchmark Where you're starting You respectfully discuss basic ideas about public policy and the social good, sharing your own opinions and acknowledging others'. You can explain basic democratic principles, the U.S. Constitution, and how individual and community involvement has shaped American government, past and present. You can describe opportunities for people or groups to engage in civic life and bring about positive change. Milestone Your target You engage with people who see public policy and the social good differently, through active listening, clear and responsive dialogue, and collaboration. You use what you know about how people's participation shapes public policy to plan for action. You make persuasive arguments that benefit society, based on your own experience, what you've observed, and outside knowledge or perspectives. The shift from Benchmark to Milestone is the shift from describing how civic life works to taking part in it: engaging with people who see things differently, and using what you notice to help move something forward.

s: The three Milestone behaviors, up close
x: The three Milestone behaviors, up close 1 Engage across different perspectives At the Benchmark level, this looks like respectful discussion: you share your view and acknowledge that others have theirs. At the Milestone level, it becomes active. You really listen to someone who sees a shared situation differently, respond to what they actually said (not what you assumed they'd say), and work with them rather than just alongside them. This is less about debate and more about something quieter. Can you be in a room, a group chat, or a shared living space with someone whose perspective is different from yours, and still move toward something together? Two roommates disagree about how guests should be handled. Benchmark: both state their position and move on. Milestone: each one listens to why the other cares, and they land on something neither started with, because they built it together. 2 Understand how participation shapes what happens At the Benchmark level, this is knowledge: you can describe how people's involvement affects what happens in a system, whether that's a government or any other shared system. At the Milestone level, you use that knowledge. You look at a situation and ask, "Given how this works, what would actually make a difference here?" This is where "civic" stops being a category of activity and becomes a way of looking at any shared space. Outcomes aren't fixed, and participation, yours and other people's, is part of what shapes them. A student notices that group projects in their program keep falling apart the same way, semester after semester. Benchmark: they can describe why. Milestone: they use that understanding to plan something different, for their own group or by raising it with an instructor in a way that could change the pattern. 3 Make a case based on real reflection At the Benchmark level, you know opportunities to make a difference exist. At the Milestone level, you can make an actual case for something, grounded in your own experience, what you've observed, and what you've learned from other perspectives. That goes beyond stating an opinion. You're building an argument someone else might find persuasive. The key word is reflection . An argument grounded in real experience and honest analysis lands differently than a generic opinion, because it's specific, and it shows your thinking, not just your conclusion. Instead of "The campus shuttle schedule doesn't work," try: "Here's specifically when and why it doesn't work for students like me, here's who else is affected, and here's what would solve it."

Where it shows up You don't need an official "civic" occasion to build these behaviors. They show up in the ordinary spaces you're already part of. A group disagrees about direction Benchmark: You share your opinion and note that others have theirs. Milestone: You listen to why others see it differently, and work toward something that reflects more than your own view. A problem keeps coming back Benchmark: You can describe the pattern and why it keeps happening. Milestone: You use that understanding to plan a different approach, for yourself or the group. Something isn't working Benchmark: You know there are ways to raise concerns or suggest change. Milestone: You build a specific case, grounded in what you've noticed, and bring it somewhere it can be heard. You notice what others miss Benchmark: You mention it in passing, if at all. Milestone: You connect what you noticed to other knowledge and perspectives, and use it to make your point land. Pathfinder Tip "Civic" doesn't have to mean "official." Every time you engage thoughtfully with people who see things differently, understand how a shared system works, and make a grounded case for something better, you're practicing civic engagement, whether or not anyone calls it that.

In your own life Reflect When was the last time you really listened to someone who saw a shared situation differently than you did? What's one problem in a space you share (home, work, class, online) that keeps coming back? If you had to make a case for one small change there, what would you say?

You're already in more communities than you think, and already shaping how they work. You're already in more communities than you might think, and you're already shaping how they work. In the last lesson, you looked at Civic Engagement and the official language behind it. This lesson is where that language stops sounding official and starts sounding like your actual life.

You're already in community When people hear "community," they often picture something big and a little distant: a city, a cause, an organization you'd have to go join. That's one kind of community, and honestly, not the most useful one to start with. Think about the spaces you're already part of: The people you live with The people you work with Your classes A team, club, or group chat Your neighborhood Online spaces and interest groups Each of these is a community. You're in several at once, and you're already shaping how they work, through what you do, what you don't do, and what you let slide. You don't have to go find community. You're already standing in it.

s: Every community runs on a system
x: Every community runs on a system What doesn't get said often enough is that every one of those spaces runs on a system. Nobody necessarily designed it on purpose, but it's there anyway. A system, in this sense, has four parts: People Who's involved, and what role each person tends to play. Rules The official ones, and the unwritten ones everyone just... knows. Influence Who actually shapes what happens. It isn't always the person with the title. Leverage points The small things that, if they changed, would change a lot else. Once you start looking for these four things, you see them everywhere. That skill reaches well beyond civic life: it helps you work out how any group you're part of operates, starting today.

Worked example: the shared kitchen Four people share a kitchen. The dishes pile up. Everyone's annoyed, but nobody's said anything. People All four are in this system, but they play different roles. Maya does dishes constantly, out of habit or because the mess bothers her most. Jordan doesn't notice the mess until someone points it out. Sam notices but figures someone else will get it. Alex is rarely home. Rules, written and unwritten The written rule might be "clean up after yourself" on a chore chart nobody follows. The unwritten rule running the show is closer to: whoever's most bothered by the mess will eventually deal with it. Nobody agreed to it. It just emerged, and everyone's behavior keeps it going. Influence Nobody's formally in charge. The person with the most real influence over whether this changes is probably Maya, not because she has authority, but because she's the one absorbing the cost, and she's most likely to shift it if she chooses to. Leverage point The obvious fix might seem like a new chore chart, but chore charts often fail because they don't touch the unwritten rule. A smaller move might work better: Maya saying, once, "Hey, I've been doing most of the dishes. Can we figure out a system together?" That makes the unwritten rule visible and gives the group a chance to choose a different one. No big confrontation, no complaint to anyone. The leverage point was naming the pattern out loud, to the people already in the room.

s: Why this counts as civic engagement
x: Why this counts as civic engagement Remember the Milestone description from the last lesson: engages with others who represent different perspectives, through active listening, clear and responsive dialogue, and collaboration. That's official language, written for a statewide rubric. But it describes exactly what happened in the kitchen. Maya didn't do anything political. She paid attention to how the situation looked to everyone, said something clear and direct, and opened the door to figuring it out together. Seeing the system, noticing who has influence (including yourself), finding the leverage point, and acting on it without making it bigger than it needs to be: those are the skills civic engagement is pointing at. They scale. The same skills that help in a shared kitchen help in a workplace, a student organization, a neighborhood association, and, eventually, civic life in the broadest sense. Look back at The 4C Check . Seeing a system clearly is the same move as Clarity and Context: step back and see what's actually going on before you react.

Your turn Pick one community you're part of right now: a living situation, a job, a class, a team, a group chat. Then work through four questions. People Who's involved, and what role does each person tend to play? Rules What's one unwritten rule running the show, something everyone seems to know even though nobody agreed to it out loud? Influence Who has the most real influence over how this community works? It might not be who you'd expect, and it might be you. Leverage point If you wanted one small thing to work better, what's one small action that might shift it? You don't need to act on any of this yet. For now, notice it, and write it down in Steps 1 and 2 of the Community Snapshot . You'll use it for Mile Marker #11. The community you pick, and what you notice about it, has to come from you.

s: If this kind of thinking interests you
x: If this kind of thinking interests you People, rules, influence, and leverage points are a small taste of systems thinking : a way of looking at almost anything, from a household to a workplace to a city or an ecosystem, and asking how its parts connect and influence each other. You don't need to study it further for this course, but if the kitchen example clicked, systems thinking is a real field with a lot more to explore, and it shows up in areas from environmental science to organizational design to public policy. s: Why "I don't have time" is usually half the story

But time is often the easy answer, because the real one is more complicated: I don't know what I'd be walking into, I don't want to let people down, and I'm worried I'd end up doing something I'd dread. That's a normal reaction to stepping into a system you can't see yet, which is what the last lesson was about. And if not knowing the system is part of what makes it hard, having your own terms clear going in makes a real difference.

s: What I have to offer, and what I don't

Not what you think you're "supposed" to offer. What I'm not available for At least for now, at least at first. A limit, a role you don't want, a kind of task that drains you. Naming both before you're in the middle of something changes the whole experience. Instead of slowly discovering your limits, and maybe feeling guilty about them, you walk in with your terms already clear, to yourself and often to the people you're working with.

None of that has been asked. It's what Jordan is bracing for. What Jordan has to offer Jordan's Module 7 results include being a steady, reliable presence and someone who notices small details, and one of their top values is being outdoors and connected to something growing. So Jordan's honest offer: "I can show up every other Saturday morning. I'm good at consistent, hands-on tasks like weeding and watering." What Jordan isn't available for "I don't want an organizing or leadership role right now. I have too much going on this semester. I'd rather just show up and do the work." Jordan says something close to this at the meeting, as an honest starting point, not a list of demands. The garden needs exactly that: reliable people doing hands-on work on a predictable schedule. Jordan wouldn't have known it was a fit, or felt comfortable saying yes, without getting clear first.

How Mile Markers are scored Every Mile Marker is scored the same way. Its rubric in Blackboard shows how many answered prompts earn each score. Full credit comes down to two things: Answer every prompt Each numbered box is one prompt. Fill in all of them. Make each answer about you Include at least one real detail from your own life, your results, or your work in the module. That's what "specific" means here. General or about you? General: "I waste time on my phone." About you: "I lose about an hour a night on my phone after my shift, so my homework starts late." The second one doesn't need to be longer or more polished. It just needs to be yours. Each prompt also has an "A strong answer" note that shows what specific looks like for that question. Honest beats polished. Your instructor won't take points off for length, spelling, or writing style. If you lose credit, your instructor will name the prompt so you know what to fix. l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · Find Your Stories
x: Prompts for every skill For the two assigned skills, these prompts help you find which moment fits. For the other eight, they're there to help something click. If one sparks a real memory, that might be your third story. Assigned: find your moment 6 Professionalism Assigned Acting with honesty and fairness, prioritizing tasks, managing time, taking initiative, and following through reliably. At its core, professionalism is being someone others can rely on: doing what you said you'd do, acting with integrity, and staying aware of how your actions affect the people around you. Think about Module 3 (your time plan) or Module 8 (your career snapshot). When did you follow through on something even though it was hard or inconvenient? When did your word matter to a classmate, coworker, or instructor, and you kept it? When did you balance what you wanted to do with what you knew was the responsible thing? 9 Knowledge Application Assigned Applying what you've learned, including academic knowledge, skills, and abilities, to real situations connected to your field or career direction. It doesn't have to be a big "aha" moment. It can be something from a class showing up somewhere outside that class: a concept that clicked once you saw it in real life, or a skill from an assignment that turned out to be useful for something else. Think about Module 6 (academic planning) or Module 8 (career exploration). When did something you learned in a class, or discovered about a career path, change how you thought about your future or what you did next? Your choice: does one of these spark something? 1 Communication Your choice Listening, weighing different perspectives, and expressing your thoughts clearly, in writing, in conversation, or in a formal setting. Real communication goes beyond the words. It includes listening, and being honest with yourself about why you're saying what you're saying: angling for something, nervous and filling space, or trying to control where a conversation goes. When did you have a conversation you weren't looking forward to: asking for help, clearing up a misunderstanding, or explaining something to someone who saw it differently? Or when did you notice something about how you were communicating, and what was driving it? 2 Critical & Creative Thinking Your choice Evaluating information and assumptions to reach informed conclusions, and combining ideas in original ways to solve problems. Part of this is being strategic instead of reactive. A lot of what competes for your attention is designed to provoke a quick reaction. Noticing that, and choosing your response anyway, is critical thinking too. Think about Module 9's 4C Check or Module 4's SIFT method. When did you slow down and think something through instead of going with your first reaction? When did you notice emotion pulling you toward a quick conclusion, and step back? 3 Quantitative Reasoning Your choice Using data, numbers, and evidence to guide decisions and choose the best approach to a problem. If "I'm bad at math" is your first reaction, you're probably using more math than you give yourself credit for: budgeting, fitting time between classes and shifts, adjusting a recipe, comparing prices. Think about Module 5 (financial planning). When did looking at actual numbers (a budget, a schedule, a pattern you tracked) change a decision? Or when did you use numbers to figure something out in everyday life, even if you wouldn't have called it math? 4 Interpersonal Relations Your choice Showing self-awareness and appreciation for different perspectives, and working respectfully with others. Think of this one as your own planet: what's going on with you in relationships, how you connect, and what you need. (Collaboration & Teamwork is the solar system: how you operate within a group.) Think about Module 2 (your support system). When did you notice something about how you connect with people, or navigate a relationship that mattered to you? 5 Adaptability & Leadership Your choice Adapting to changing circumstances, finding ways to work and thrive in different settings, and supporting others toward a shared goal. Leadership doesn't have to mean team captain or club president. It also means leading your own life: making decisions, taking responsibility for your choices, or stepping up in a small way without anyone assigning you the role. Sometimes it's just becoming someone others quietly look to because of how you handled something. Starting college is itself a major adjustment. Was there a moment early this semester when you had to adapt to something that caught you off guard? Or think about Module 3 (time and energy) or Module 10 (collaboration): when did something change unexpectedly, and how did you adjust? When did you lead yourself, or quietly help a group move forward? 7 Civic Engagement Your choice Taking part in activities, political, social, or otherwise, that address issues and benefit a shared community. There's a saying often associated with Gandhi: "Be the change you want to see in the world." It doesn't have to mean something huge. It can mean noticing a gap in a community you're part of and helping close it. Think about Module 11 and your Mile Marker #11. When were you part of that kind of change, even informally? Or how do you want to start being that kind of presence, building on your offer and boundary? 8 Collaboration & Teamwork Your choice Working effectively in teams, being an effective team member, and managing conflict constructively. Where Interpersonal Relations is your own planet, this one is the solar system: how you operate within a group, and how everyone's orbits affect each other. Think about Module 10 (your collaboration profile). Almost everyone has a group work story, and it's not always a good one. A project that went sideways often makes a better story than a smooth one, especially if you can point to something you did or learned because of it. 10 Information Literacy Your choice Identifying,

l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · What Makes a Strong Story
x: How stories are scored You get credit for each STAR(T) step you complete. A step counts when it's there and it's about you. Step It counts when it... Situation Sets the scene: where, when, and what was going on. Task Says what you needed to do or solve. Action Says what you did, not only what "we" did. Result Says what happened because of what you did. Transfer Names where you'll use this skill next. A response that isn't a true story about you, or doesn't use STAR(T), doesn't earn credit. Recorded stories are never scored on delivery, only on the story and its structure.

s: Three fixes that make a story stronger
l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · What Makes a Strong Story
x: Three fixes that make a story stronger Swap "we" for "I" Before We reorganized the schedule so everyone could make it. After I asked each person for their work hours, built a new schedule around them, and sent it to the group that night. Make the Result concrete Before It went really well. After Everyone made the next three meetings, and we turned the project in a day early. Name where the Transfer goes Before This will help me in my future career. After In clinicals next year I'll be coordinating with nurses on different shifts, and I now know to ask about everyone's constraints before I plan.

s: This isn't a public speaking class
l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · Tell It Out Loud
x: This isn't a public speaking class Recordings are not graded on delivery or presentation . No one is scoring your eye contact, your voice, your lighting, or your camera. They're scoring your story and its structure. It only needs to be clear enough to follow. If you stumble, keep going. Interviewers don't expect polish either. They listen for honesty, structure, and a clear point.

l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · Tell It Out Loud
x: The rambling problem Even experienced professionals ramble when they're nervous. They back up to add context, circle around the point, and suddenly realize they've talked for four minutes without reaching the Action. That's nerves, not a lack of preparation. A tight two-minute story that hits all five steps beats a wandering seven-minute one. To get there, know your story before you hit record. Read your practice guide out loud at least once. Know where each step starts and ends. Then trust the structure. What 2 to 4 minutes looks like Situation 20 to 30 seconds Two or three sentences. Don't linger. Task 15 to 20 seconds Your role or challenge, in a sentence or two. Action 60 to 90 seconds Spend most of your time here. Use "I." Result 20 to 30 seconds What specifically happened. Transfer 30 to 45 seconds Where this skill shows up next. Pathfinder Tip Practice once with a timer. Running long? Your Action or your Situation is doing too much. Trim the Situation first. Each practice guide also estimates how long your draft runs out loud.

l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · Your Capstone Assignment
x: Why this matters beyond FYE 100 Saying "I'm a hard worker" is easy. Showing it with a real story is what makes people believe you. You'll be asked for that kind of story again and again: In job interviews. Many employers ask behavioral questions that start with "Tell me about a time when..." A STAR story is the answer they're listening for. In applications. Scholarships, competitive programs like many health programs, and transfer applications often ask you to describe a real experience. At work. Performance reviews, promotions, and references all come down to examples of what you actually did. The skills you'll show are the 10 Essential Skills, the same ones every public college in Kentucky, including OCTC, builds its programs around. By the end of this course you'll have three true stories, practiced out loud, that you can adapt for any of those moments.
