l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · The STAR(T) Framework
x: Five steps for telling the story of a skill you've actually built. Anyone can claim a skill. A STAR(T) story shows it. STAR comes from behavioral interviewing, the method many employers use when they want to know not just what you know, but what you've actually done. When an interviewer says "Tell me about a time when...", they're asking for a STAR story. "I'm a hard worker" is a claim. A specific story is evidence. This course adds one more step, Transfer, the (T). It turns a good story into a reflection on where you're headed.

l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · The STAR(T) Framework
x: The five steps S Situation: set the scene Briefly describe where you were and what was happening. Give just enough background for someone who wasn't there. What was going on? Watch out: don't linger. The Situation is setup, not the story. T Task: define your role What were you responsible for? What were you trying to accomplish, and why was it yours to handle? What did you need to do, and why was it on you? Watch out: your task is your part, not the group's general goal. A Action: show what you did The most important step. Use "I": I decided, I reached out, I applied, I chose. Describe what you did, not what the team did or what happened in general. The Action is where the skill lives. What did you specifically do, step by step? Watch out: "we" hides your contribution. Describe your part, even in a group effort. R Result: name the outcome What happened because of what you did? Results don't have to be perfect. An honest, imperfect result is more believable than a vague positive one. What happened, and what did it mean? Watch out: "It went well" isn't a result. Name what changed. T Transfer: connect it forward So what? What does this experience mean for your next semester, your career, or your life beyond college? This is what makes a STAR(T) story a reflection, not just a story. What does this mean for what comes next? Watch out: "This will help me in the future" isn't a Transfer. Say where, when, and how. Key Term Behavioral interview: a job interview built on "Tell me about a time when..." questions, where your past actions are the evidence. Why the T? Standard STAR ends with the Result, which is enough for an interview. Transfer shows you learned from the experience and know where you're taking it. It's the hardest step for most students, and the one that most sets a strong story apart.

l: STAR(T) Stories Guide · The STAR(T) Framework
x: What it looks like Below is a complete STAR(T) story with Knowledge Application as the focus skill. 9 Example: Knowledge Application Situation I was working as a medical receptionist when a patient came in upset about a billing error. The front desk staff weren't sure how to handle it, and the office manager wasn't available. Task I needed to help with the patient's concern without making promises I couldn't keep, and without making things worse while we waited for the manager. Action I used what I'd learned in my Medical Billing course about how insurance claims are processed to explain what likely caused the problem. I pulled up her account, walked her through the codes that had been submitted, and explained what the next step in the review would be, without guessing at the outcome. Result The patient calmed down and agreed to wait for the manager to follow up with the insurance company. She thanked me for taking the time to explain what was happening instead of just telling her to wait. Transfer It showed me that what I'm learning in my Healthcare Administration program isn't just for passing tests. It's for moments like that one, when a real person needs someone who understands the system. I'm going to keep asking, in every course: what does this knowledge look like when it matters? Pathfinder Tip Your story doesn't have to be dramatic. A quiet moment at work, in class, or with your family is exactly what STAR(T) is built for. Specific and honest beats impressive and polished.
